entries.title: The Brewers own the Cubs — it's just reality
entries.summary: <p>Another year, another “own” goal in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>-Brewers rivalry.</p><p>Actually, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/20/brewers-cubs-jacob-misiorowski-christian-yelich-pete-crow-armstrong-wrigley-field-mlb" target="_blank" >make that the Brewers-Cubs rivalry</a>. No doubt, the Brewers deserve to be named first. There’s no team they enjoy leaving in the National League Central dust more than the Cubs, and wouldn’t you know it? They’ve all but done it again.</p><p>There’s no easy or nice way to say it, but it’s the truth: The North-of-the-Border Nine owns our North Siders.</p><p>The Brewers showed up Monday for the opener of a four-game series at Wrigley Field with the best record in the big leagues and a bullyish eight-game lead over the second-place Cubs, who almost certainly will soon be 0-for-3 in the division-winning department since Craig Counsell switched sides to become the sport’s first $8 million-a-year manager.</p><p>Worse than that, it stands to be the eighth straight full season — the exception being the pandemic-shortened 60-game sprint in 2020 — in which the Cubs will finish behind the Brewers, who are closing in on their sixth division crown during the most dominant stretch of baseball in franchise history.</p><p>“Look, we get 13 chances to play the Brewers,” Counsell said, his team off to a 2-4 start in the season series. “And other than that, we don’t have any control over the Brewers. They’ve got to go play their games, and we go play our games.”</p><p>If the implication is that the rivals’ records might be closer if they played each other 162 times, it’s hard to fathom why they would be.</p><p>“They’re on pace for a big number — they’re on over a 100-win pace — and that’s hard to keep up with,” Counsell said. “Go ask the rest of major league baseball.”</p><p>No one in Cubdom has to ask anybody. To put the bullying in perspective, think back to the mercilessly one-sided decades of Brett Favre, Aaron Rodgers and the Packers owning the Bears and know the last time the Packers had the better record eight times in nine years was from 1992 to 2000. Still too fresh for Bears fans, no doubt, but kind of a long time ago.</p><p>Counsell didn’t come here to lose to his former team. His boss, Jed Hoyer, didn’t stake his own reputation on an all-in managerial hire just to go oh-fer in division races. Counsell has a couple of years left after this one, and the Cubs are positioned to continue to be a playoff-caliber team. But there’s no sign of the Brewers losing their mojo and fading away.</p><p>I asked Counsell how disappointed and/or frustrated he is that the Cubs haven’t been able to close the gap on his watch.</p><p>“ ‘Disappointed’ is not the right word,” he said. “They’re good. They’re a good team. I’m not surprised by that, not surprised at all. We’re a good team. We’re not a 100-win team — we’re not going to be a 100-win team this year — but we’re a good team. So that’s the story right now, and we’ve got games in front of us.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The <a href="https://x.com/Cubs?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Cubs</a> go back-to-back!<br><br>Now Nico Hoerner leaves the yard 💪 <a href="https://t.co/P55cpzyhuS">https://t.co/P55cpzyhuS</a> <a href="https://t.co/DKEgZ6pb6b">pic.twitter.com/DKEgZ6pb6b</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2094575296594788766?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 31, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Cubs finished 10 games behind the Brewers and missed the playoffs in 2024, Counsell’s first season. The gap was smaller — five games — last year, but the Brewers’ postseason series win against the Cubs underscored an undeniable hierarchy.</p><p>This season, the low point for the Cubs was a 10-game losing streak in May during which they were swept by the Brewers in three lopsided games — combined score, 19-5 — at Wrigley. The Brewers torched starter Shota Imanaga for eight earned runs in an opening 9-3 win that was reminiscent, right down to the final score, of the Brewers’ 9-3 win in Game 1 of last year’s NL division series, when they jumped on starter Matthew Boyd and the Cubs for six first-inning runs. Both games were like early-years Mike Tyson knockouts.</p><p>As Brewers manager Pat Murphy told his players going into that playoff series, “When the bell rings, you’re ready. You don’t get a couple rounds to figure out whether or not you want to fight.”</p><p>Before the Cubs’ 10-game losing streak this year, they were in first place by 2½ games over the Brewers. By the end of it, they were in last place, 4½ games behind an uncanny powerhouse that never seems to fail to take advantage of openings and opportunities. The same has happened as the Cubs hit a little 3-7 jag entering the teams’ current series; over that same period, the Brewers kept plowing ahead at 7-3, doubling their lead from four to eight.</p><p>On the eve of Opening Day this season, I spoke with Christian Yelich, the longest-tenured Brewer, in Milwaukee. As is the case most years, the Cubs were projected to win more games. Yelich scoffed.</p><p>“I think a lot of people have been really waiting for the day that we suck and they can finally say, ‘We told you so, they’re no good,’ ” he said. “We’ve become accustomed to winning and being a postseason team. … That’s definitely not changing this year.”</p><p>Murphy — who has an excellent shot at a third straight NL manager of the year award — wasn’t backing down from a brawl in the slightest, either, five months ago.</p><p>“Buckle up and get ready,” he said, “because it’s going to be a fight. There’ll be a lot of bloodshed and pain to get to where you want to go.”</p><p>It sometimes seems the Cubs are less driven than the Brewers are to finish at the top of the standings.</p><p>“I think what motivates our group is playing good baseball and winning as many games as we can, and that’s been a constant since we’ve been together,” Ian Happ, the longest-tenured Cub, said Monday. “It’s always kind of the guiding light. You want to win divisions. You really want to win divisions — it means a lot — but playoff baseball is the important part.”</p><p>But the bullies have the Cubs bloodied again.</p><p>Getting a bit old, is it not?</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/31/cubs-brewers-phillies-nl-central-nl-wild-card-standings-diamondbacks-padres-mlb-playoffs-first-round" >Next two weeks give Cubs opportunity to make NL Central push vs. Brewers, but wild-card fate in balance, too</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/20/brewers-cubs-jacob-misiorowski-christian-yelich-pete-crow-armstrong-wrigley-field-mlb" >It’s Reality Week at Wrigley Field, where determined Brewers outclassed Cubs. What else is new?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/10/11/cubs-2025-postseason-runs-with-game-5-loss-to-brewers-in-nld" target="_blank" >Cubs’ 2025 postseason run ends with Game 5 loss to Brewers in NLDS</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Man fatally shot on Lower West Side
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot Monday evening on the Lower West Side, police said.</p><p>The man, 35, was sitting on the front porch of a residence in the 2300 block of West 18th Place just before 7 p.m. when a car approached and someone got out and fired shots, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital with gunshot wounds to the chest. He was pronounced dead at the hospital.</p><p>No one is in custody and detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: After competing for a rotation spot in spring, Sean Newcomb has been invaluable in White Sox bullpen
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – Protecting a one-run lead for four innings on Saturday, with relief ace Grant Taylor unavailable after working a career-high 2 2/3 frames on Friday, there were no easy answers for White Sox manager Will Venable.</p><p>Unless the answer was a lot of Sean Newcomb.</p><p>“I was talking with [general manager’ Chris Getz about it yesterday, about how valuable these guys are,” said Venable. “[Newcomb] leads the way. That prototype of pitchers, where he’s really good, he takes the ball all the time and [is] giving me two or three innings when he does pitch. It’s special.”</p><p>For the third time this year, and the second-straight outing, Newcomb posted three scoreless innings, helping push the Sox to 24-20 in one-run games. Newcomb’s logged 11 outings since he last allowed an earned run, spanning 20 1/3 innings. The streak has dropped his season ERA to 2.19, while working the third-most relief innings in the American League.</p><p>“You come out of the game and you see him coming in, you feel good about it,” said Sox starter Sean Burke.</p><p>An exciting young offensive core has powered this Sox team to the AL Central lead. But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/white-sox-manager-will-venable-excited-to-bring-tommy-pham-jordan-leasure-mike-vasil-jose-urquidy-chris-getz-jake-cave-tyler-schweitzer-brenton-doyle-everson-pereira" target="_blank" ><u>Jordan Leasure and Mike Vasil were lost to season-ending elbow injuries</u></a> after being valuable setup men last year. Free-agent signing Seranthony Domínguez washed out as closer before being flipped at the deadline. Fireballer Jordan Hicks spent most of the first half battling a lat strain and searching for the right arm slot.</p><p>Protecting the leads of the AL’s best offense would be a tricky problem without a 33-year-old left-hander signed to a one-year, $4.5 million deal just before last Christmas, putting together arguably his finest season.</p><p>“Numbers-wise, can’t argue that,” Newcomb told the Sun-Times. “I'd say it’s a continuation of what I started doing with the A's when I got to a full-time bullpen job last year.”</p><p>Newcomb posted a 1.75 ERA in 51 1/3 innings for the A’s, after being designated for assignment midseason by his hometown Boston Red Sox, who had been using him as more of a spot starter/swingman. He credits that experience for why he has the stamina to maintain his performance even while on pace for over 90 innings this year.</p><p>What deserves possibly more credit is that in his 10th MLB season, on his fifth MLB team, after plenty of years dogged by injury and/or struggles, Newcomb is unfazed by anything.</p><p>“It’s been a new mindset I’ve had with pitching since I got back to playing consistently,” Newcomb said. “Just approaching every pitch the same way, no matter what it is.”</p><p>At a long-limbed six-foot-five and throwing from a lower arm slot than earlier in his career, Newcomb splits the plate horizontally with his slurve and a new sinker. That east-west dynamic has helped make the letter-high four-seam fastballs he peppers in to change eye levels one of the most effective pitches in the sport.</p><p>Part of Newcomb’s extended relief excellence are tools usually reserved for starters. When the situation calls for a groundball, or when it calls for a strikeout, Newcomb can hunt for either. When he misfires a four-seamer, he gets back into the count with a sinker, or vice-versa. Forget about his curveball, changeup or cutter, and that’s when they might appear.</p><p>For all the problems he’s solved in relief, maybe he would have done pretty well in that rotation job he wanted and competed for in spring.</p><p>“I haven’t weighed that in my head,” conceded Venable. “You have the argument to make that case. At the same time, he’s been so good and helped us win so many games, we are utilizing him well.”</p><p>But Newcomb is set to hit free agency again this winter, a forum where starting is markedly more valuable than relieving. Surely he’s more convinced in his ability to do the former than ever?</p><p>“No, same as always,” said Newcomb, true to his mindset.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Cubs’ aggressive additions could prove key to finally clearing Brewers-shaped hurdle, now or in October
entries.summary: <p>If you can’t beat ‘em, add ‘em?</p><p>Even after luring <b>Craig Counsell</b> away, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> have yet to wrest control of the division from the Brewers.</p><p>But with another ex-Brewer in the fold, maybe things could be different?</p><p><b>Tyrone Taylor</b>, a Brewer from 2019 to 2023, made the case with his first-inning home run Monday, the start of a Cubs home-run barrage in the opener of the teams’ four-game series.</p><p>Taylor was added in one of <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >aggressive moves at the trade deadline</a>, that deal with the Mets landing Monday’s starter, <b>Clay Holmes</b>, with hopes of the righty propelling the Cubs to big things from the top of the rotation.</p><p>Hoyer & Co. likely weren’t thinking of Taylor, a reserve outfielder who brought a .368 average and a .432 on-base percentage as a Cub into Monday, as a middle-of-the-order presence, but that homer – his first in a Cubs uniform – came from the cleanup spot.</p><p>Sure, role players can be difference-makers, but the Cubs parted with No. 2 prospect <b>Jefferson Rojas</b> to nab Holmes, who looked worth the cost once more Monday, following up <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-walk-off-loss-diamondbacks-clay-holmes-kevin-gausman-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-bullpen" >seven shutout innings against the Diamondbacks</a> with six more scoreless frames against the Brewers. He’s got a 1.55 ERA since being acquired.</p><p>Before all that, the Cubs spent $175 million to add third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b>, whose <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/21/cubs-alex-bregman-playoffs-stats-world-series-dansby-swanson-carson-kelly-craig-counsell" >scorching summer</a> has only been overshadowed by <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b>’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/29/cubs-star-pete-crow-armstrong-hits-three-home-runs-to-bolster-mvp-case" >MVP push</a>. Bregman had a .967 OPS in his previous 42 games before homering twice in his first three at-bats Monday.</p><p>If the Cubs are going to finally clear the Brewers-shaped hurdle, be it in a surprise late-season rally in the division race or come the postseason, the front office’s aggressive work to add to the roster could prove the difference.</p><p><b>Sticking with Shota</b></p><p>The Cubs have no plans to remove lefty <b>Shota Imanaga</b> from their rotation following <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/30/chicago-cubs-shota-imanaga-three-homers-cincinnati-reds-craig-counsell-jody-davis-jon-lester-ed-howard-edward-cabrera" >a second straight clunker Sunday</a>.</p><p>Imanaga leaped into a tie for the major league lead in home runs allowed by surrendering a trio to the Reds, matching the 33 given up by <b>Jeffrey Springs</b> of the Athletics.</p><p>“Shota’s going to make his next start,” Counsell said Monday. “We’re going to continue to work on, like everybody, having him be more effective, be your best possible self and be as effective as you possibly can. That work never stops.</p><p>“We need Shota to be one of our guys.”</p><p>The choice to stick with Imanaga is no shock. Though he wrapped a rough August with a 5.96 ERA in five starts, including a pair of games in which he allowed three homers, that followed a terrific July (1.53 ERA in five starts) and a stretch of a 2.09 ERA in nine starts.</p><p>“Major League Baseball is an execution game,” Counsell said. “Shota has proven, at his best self, he’s a very good major league pitcher. He didn’t execute some things [Sunday] night.”</p><p>However, watching Imanaga serve up long balls brings to mind how his 2025 ended: He gave up 10 homers in September and wasn’t chosen to start the Cubs’ loss to the Brewers in Game 5 of the NLDS.</p><p><b>Murray? Present.</b></p><p>Infielder <b>B.J. Murray Jr.</b> is joining the Cubs after putting up impressive numbers in the minors this season.</p><p>In 118 games with Triple-A Iowa, Murray hit .294/.395/.500 with 49 extra-base hits, 68 RBIs and 74 runs scored.</p><p>Murray, ranked as the organization’s No. 19 prospect, was a 15th-round draft choice of the Cubs in 2021.</p><p>He’ll become the second player born in the Bahamas to appear in a game for the Cubs, joining infielder <b>Andre Rodgers</b>, who played in nearly 500 games across four seasons as a North Sider in the 1960s.</p>

entries.title: Indiana's governor demands probe of power utility during tour of storm-ravaged Gary
entries.summary: <p>Brenda Medema grabbed lunch Monday afternoon at the American Red Cross Shelter inside the Hudson Campbell Sports and Fitness Center in downtown Gary.</p><p>The shelter became her home soon after a storm ripped through Northwest Indiana on Aug. 11.</p><p>“It’s been really tough," said Medema, 57. "I was getting heatstroke. I’ve been living in the shelter but the Red Cross makes it worth it."</p><p>Thousands lost power for days following the storm. While most have had it restored, dozens remained without power.</p><p>At the shelter, Indiana Gov. Mike Braun continued calls for a probe of the area's utility company after he made his tour of Gary. He also visited the area the day after the storm.</p><p>“We've never had this kind of an event in 100 years,” Braun said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Whole Foods planned for vacant Treasure Island building in Old Town
entries.summary: <p>A new Whole Foods Market is planned to open in Old Town, according to the neighborhood's alderperson. </p><p>The grocery store chain recently signed a lease at the former Treasure Island Foods location, 2nd Ward Ald. Brian Hopkins announced Monday in his weekly newsletter. The building at 1639 N. Wells St. has sat vacant since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/9/29/18441977/chicago-grocery-chain-treasure-island-foods-to-shut-down-after-55-years" target="_blank" >Treasure Island closed in 2018</a>. </p><p>An opening date has not been determined, Hopkins said in a statement. </p><p>“From the beginning of the redevelopment review, I was clear that restoring a full-service grocery store to this location had to be a priority," he said. “Whole Foods Market is an established operator with the capacity to serve the neighborhood for the long term. There is still work ahead, but the signed lease is a concrete and welcome step forward.”</p><p>The grocery store chain also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/04/20/whole-foods-grocery-store-wicker-park-lake-view" target="_blank" >plans to open stores</a> in the Wicker Park and Lake View neighborhoods.</p>
entries.author: Kaitlin Washburn

entries.title: White Sox manager Will Venable excited to bring Tommy Pham's trademark 'edge' to young, contending roster
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – Right-hander <b>Tanner McDougal</b>, a preseason top-100 prospect per <i>Baseball America </i>capable of touching 100 mph, was in the visitor’s locker room at Daikin Park on Monday and will be activated on Tuesday as part of MLB rosters expanding to 28 players.</p><p>There’s more focus on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/tyler-schweitzer-tyler-gilbert-white-sox-davis-martin-will-venable-kyle-teel-ryan-fuller-astros-series-houston" target="_blank" ><u>the other player expected to join the Sox</u></a> on Tuesday: a 38-year-old platoon corner outfielder acquired from the Phillies Triple-A squad for cash.</p><p>Over his 13 MLB seasons, <b>Tommy Pham</b> has a career .796 OPS against left-handed pitching. He addresses a need for right-handed thump created when the Sox designated both <b>Everson Pereira</b> and <b>Austin Hays</b> for assignment within days of each other to make room trade-deadline acquisition <b>Brenton Doyle</b>; a glove-first center fielder.</p><p>The Sox have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/21/white-sox-tristan-peters-second-half-slump-all-star-game-brenton-doyle-davis-martin-kyle-teel-will-venable-derek-shomon-mets-luis-robert-jr" target="_blank" ><u>plans for unlocking more offense from Doyle in the future</u></a>, but a long and durable offensive track record is the heart of Pham’s appeal. The 38-year-old is a .315/.331/.492 hitter in 37 career playoff games.</p><p>“He understands what it means to be in meaningful games down the stretch,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>. “He knows what it means to play playoff games. He understands what it means to just perform and exist in high-leverage situations.”</p><p>Beyond the field, Pham is more famous both publicly and in league circles for his marked intensity. His 2024 stint with the White Sox is remembered less for him being the only Sox regular with an OPS over the league average, and more for him <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/06/02/tommy-pham-fighting-mad-after-white-sox-11th-straight-loss" target="_blank" ><u>overtly criticizing coaching decisions and touting his hand-to-hand combat skills</u></a> after an on-field dustup with Brewers All-Star catcher William Contreras after a grueling loss in Milwaukee.</p><p>Rather than worrying how Pham will mesh with his young roster and their deliriously goofy dugout hijinks, Venable is looking forward to it.</p><p>“One of my favorite players to coach,” said Venable, who overlapped with Pham as the Red Sox bench coach in 2022. “There’s a real value to how he approaches things, and that edge that he’s got is real. I think it also works in a lot of different types of environments; I think our environment, especially.”</p><p><b>Leasure out until 2028</b></p><p>Sox reliever <b>Jordan Leasure</b> faced a long road to recovery when he was sidelined with a flexor strain in late May. He’s now looking at an even longer one after undergoing surgery to repair a torn ulnar collateral ligament on Aug. 17. The Sox are hoping Leasure can return by spring 2028.</p><p>After undergoing his own UCL repair this spring, <b>Mike Vasil</b> is traveling to visit Dr. Keith Meister on Tuesday for a progress assessment. Pending approval, he should begin throwing mid-September.</p><p><b>This and that</b></p><p><b>Tyler Schweitzer </b>was activated from the paternity list Monday after missing this weekend’s series in Minneapolis. He has a 3.64 ERA in 29 2/3 innings of relief, and took <b>Tyler Gilbert</b>’s spot on the roster.</p><p>Rather than be a Sept. 1 addition, <b>Drew Thorpe</b> will start for Triple-A Charlotte on Wednesday.</p><p>The Sox also acquired veteran outfielder <b>Jake Cave</b> from the Rays for cash. Cave, 33, has not appeared in the majors since 2024.</p><p>A veteran of three separate Astros’ World Series runs, <b>Jose Urquidy </b>was greeted as a returning postseason hero in his first trip back to Houston since 2023.</p><p>“They [taught] me how to be a good professional baseball player,” Urquidy said. “And I’m very grateful.”</p>

entries.title: Bears move S Coby Bryant, TE Hayden Large to injured reserve, sign DT James Lynch to active roster
entries.summary: <p>The Bears didn’t make any moves Monday, but some roster-shuffling is coming.</p><p>The team had only one of the 22 players it waived Sunday claimed by another team — offensive lineman Mason Murphy went to the Saints — and will want to bring at least some of them back, whether on the practice squad or on the active roster.</p><p>Safety Coby Bryant and backup tight end Hayden Large got hurt during training camp, so both needed to count toward the 53-man roster limit Sunday to have a chance to play this season. After the initial roster cuts, however, they can move to injured reserve and open roster spots.</p><p>The Bears also will have to weigh the health of left tackle Ozzy Trapilo, defensive end Austin Booker and running back Kyle Monangai and whether they expect them to be back within the first four games.</p><p>Nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon and defensive lineman Shemar Turner were on the physically unable-to-perform list before camp and stayed on it Sunday, ruling them out for the first four games.</p><p>The team plans to re-sign defensive tackle James Lynch, who was released Sunday, a source said.</p><p>The Bears also signed 11 players to practice-squad contracts, including veteran defensive end Marcus Davenport and wide receiver Scotty Miller, as well as wide receiver Kaden Davis, who has been a standout in camp.</p><p>Offensive lineman Kiran Amegadjie, a third-round pick in 2024, agreed to a practice-squad deal with the Eagles, a source said.</p>

entries.title: Stand by Second Amendment but don't deny damage guns can cause
entries.summary: <p>When I was a boy two brothers lived on our block and we ran together every weekend. Ball in the street, made-up games, War!</p><p>Then one day they were gone. My buddy said their father had lost his job at the tire factory and taken his own life in the basement with a gun the family owned.</p><p>That was a gun death in America. Quiet street, good schools. In all my years arguing guns, a death like that almost never came up.</p><p>Our children are back in school, and September is Suicide Prevention Month.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bb0000" name="module-bb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Guns, children and despair are one subject. We rarely treat them so.</p><p>My friend Lenny McAllister has never made me pick. He is a Black Republican, a voice on Rust Belt radio from WVON in Chicago to KDKA in Pittsburgh. I was the Democratic nominee for governor of Maryland. We have gone at each other's parties 20 years and stayed friends.</p><p>What people miss is that we are both civil rights men, and civil rights work is Bill of Rights work.</p><p>The First Amendment is why we could march. The Fourth Amendment is why an officer needs a reason to search you. The Second Amendment sits in that same document, and we believe in all of it.</p><p>Lenny's father was shot on a Rust Belt street and spent nearly a year in the hospital. In 2001 a man broke into Lenny's home and tied him up. He tells it in his new book, "A Venn Diagram of One," an honest book about refusing to be one thing in a country that insists you choose.</p><p>My cousin was shot and killed at a gas station in Columbia, Maryland, at noon. A cousin I called uncle agreed to testify against a Prince George's County drug dealer, who shot him at his door. He lived. At the hospital they would not let us up to his room, for fear the shooter's friends would come finish the job.</p><p>When Lenny writes that we can respect the Second Amendment and still use common sense about who buys a gun, I hear no man splitting a difference. I hear a man who has waited on word about his father, and lain on his own floor with a gun at his head.</p><p>Then he writes this. "There is a right greater than the right to bear arms; it is the right to a liberty-filled life."</p><p>Now let me tell you what I got wrong.</p><p>Thirty years ago at Oxford I needed a thesis topic. A headline in the International Herald Tribune stopped me on the sidewalk. Black teen suicides were surging. I was sure I knew why. Handguns were flooding the inner cities.</p><p>I was wrong. The children dying were not in the cities. They were in the suburbs.</p><p>Black families moved out there in the late '60s and '70s. Twenty years later their children began killing themselves. Children like me, with the big backyard and the shiny bike.</p><p>Our mothers gave us what they had been denied in the projects and tenements and row houses they came up in. Without meaning to, they cost us the one thing those places had, a house full of family who would listen no matter what.</p><p>One of the strongest predictors of a suicide attempt is isolation. Ask a woman how many people she talks to after her worst day and she names two or three. Ask a man and he names one, or nobody. Her circle grows all her life. His shrinks toward zero.</p><p>That headline should have said the Black teen suicide rate was catching up to the White one. Among young Black men it has passed it.</p><p>About nine in 10 suicide attempts with a gun end in death. With most other methods people live, and most who live never die by suicide.</p><p>In 2024 there were 27,593 gun suicides, well over half of all gun deaths.</p><p>Money is no shield. A gun in a cul-de-sac is as final as a gun on a corner.</p><p>The Bill of Rights is not a menu. You do not get to order the Second Amendment and send the rest back to the kitchen. None of it means much to a child who does not live to grow into the promise of life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.</p><p>So set partisanship aside. Lock your own guns in a safe at home. Keep them away from people in crisis. And build friendships across party lines that bind this nation back together for all our children.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b80000" name="module-b80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Ben Jealous

entries.title: Dear Abby: Oldest sibling needs help with widowed mom
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My father passed away three months ago, leaving my mom alone for the first time in her life. She lives nearby, so my wife and I have been doing what we can. We have her over several times a week, and we visit and call to check in often.</p><p>Mom is having a hard time and sometimes forgets to eat or get dressed if we don't remind her. There has been a lot of legal stuff to do following Dad's death, decisions she's not up for, so we're doing that, too. I'm trying to get her professional help (counseling and help at home), but there are waiting lists, and it's going to take time. I'm also mourning Dad, and it's been a lot.</p><p>What I'd really like is for my brothers to step up. One lives in the next town. The other is only a couple of hours away. Neither one has been to see Mom since the funeral, and it doesn't sound like they've been calling her often.</p><p>I'm the oldest, and they are used to me taking care of things, but this is more than I can handle alone. I have told them that directly. They both say they want to help, but then they don't. I have tried giving them specific tasks (for example, to call Mom in the morning before 10 on a certain day), and they agree but then don't follow through. We usually get along.</p><p>They are both successful people with good jobs and families, so I don't understand why they are slacking here. I think they're just used to Mom being the caretaker and can't see that the roles are reversed now even though we're all in our 40s and no longer little boys. How do I get them to start shouldering their share of the responsibility here? — <i>IN CHARGE IN WISCONSIN</i></p><p><b>DEAR IN CHARGE:</b> Because your brothers cannot be trusted to step up and give your mother more time, there is another way they can take some of the responsibility off your shoulders. They can offer money in lieu of time. Each could chip in so that their mother has a caregiver or companion to help her with the household chores. They should also contribute toward grief or psychological counseling until she is stronger. If you suggest all of that, you may find they magically begin calling Mom more often!</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am at my wits' end. I support myself and my boyfriend of 14 years. I have no extra money to support anyone else. My boyfriend's mother, who is our neighbor, treats him like a dog and always has. She constantly asks him for stuff. He gives her things that I have worked for — cigarettes, soft drinks, food, etc. It all adds up, and I can't do it anymore. Please give me any advice that you have. — <i>TIRED</i></p><p><b>DEAR TIRED:</b> You have learned the hard way that your boyfriend and his mom are a package deal, and they are both deadbeats. Get out of there and stop letting them use you. Find a place of your own, block his calls, and experience the satisfaction of living on your own. Once you've done that, I'm sure you can find yourself a much better man — or you may decide you don't need one.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Failed inspections, bodies parked on a suburban street — the troubled history behind South Chicago Chapel
entries.summary: <p>The tax bills piled up for years on an Evergreen Park couple that ran a sprawling network of crematory and funeral services across the South Side and suburbs.</p><p>So did a series of professional disciplinary cases against Clark and Johanna Morgan, along with a bizarre run-in with police who found two bodies in the back of a minivan outside their home. And that was before authorities discovered dozens of mishandled corpses at their now-shuttered Chicago Heights crematory.</p><p>But none of those apparent red flags proved enough to prevent another gruesome discovery of 56 unrefrigerated, decomposing bodies this summer inside the couple’s South Chicago Chapel, a building that had its own troubled history with city inspectors long before the Morgans acquired it.</p><p>A WBEZ/Sun-Times review of public records underscores the tangled web of oversight responsibilities across multiple levels of government that officials are grappling with to prevent the emergence of another <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice" target="_blank" ><u>nightmare scenario</u></a> in the state’s mortuary industry.</p><p>“Where you have multiple departments within the city and multiple governments that are responsible, routinely there's a giant question of who's actually in charge, because everybody tends to stick to their core mission and operational mandates and not coordinate well,” said former Chicago inspector general Joe Ferguson, who now leads the nonpartisan Civic Federation. “Somebody needs to be driving that bigger train.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/10/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-oversight-illinois-decomposing-bodies" >The case has prompted state lawmakers</a> to reconsider arbitrary divisions of funeral industry regulation in Illinois, which is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/18/south-deering-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-illinois-lax-oversight-inspections" >one of just four states </a>that don't conduct regular inspections of funeral homes. </p><h3></h3><h3><b>Years of failed inspections</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The property that houses South Chicago Chapel hadn’t been inspected by the city’s Buildings Department in the four years leading up to the discovery, the entire time the Morgans operated their business at 2939 E. 95th St.</p><p>City inspection records show that after 15 years of failing nearly every annual building department inspection from 2006 to 2021, annual inspections abruptly stopped in 2022. That’s the year South Chicago Chapel was created, a year before its owners bought the building.</p><p>When asked why annual inspections stopped in 2022, a Buildings Department spokesperson pointed to a fact sheet outlining the department’s apparent shift from annual inspections to a priority-based inspection process. The spokesperson added that the building department is only responsible for inspecting areas used for public assembly, such as funerals or wakes, not private embalming areas where the bodies were found.</p><p>“A DOB annual inspection would not have covered these restricted areas and could not have revealed the tragic circumstances discovered within them,” the spokesperson said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/30/south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-funeral-home-vigil-families" >Families call for criminal charges for South Chicago Chapel owners</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But it’s clear from reports after the early August discovery that an inspector would not have had to enter an embalming room to know that something was terribly wrong.</p><p>“Upon entry, city and state officials encountered a strong, foul, and putrid odor consistent with decomposition of human remains throughout the building,” a Business Affairs and Consumer Protection report stated.</p><p>From 2006 to 2021, the property — which has long housed funeral homes — was receiving annual inspections and failed nearly every one. Half the time, it was because inspectors weren’t given access to the building, and because of small exterior violations. Other times, it was due to a series of minor violations inside.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fc0000" name="image-fc0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9b73c1a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6280x3524+0+476/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F11%2Fff26614d42989f7645a8d130843b%2Ffuneralhomesmell-260814-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ebe4e77/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6280x3524+0+476/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F11%2Fff26614d42989f7645a8d130843b%2Ffuneralhomesmell-260814-6.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/752769f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6280x3524+0+476/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F11%2Fff26614d42989f7645a8d130843b%2Ffuneralhomesmell-260814-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The boarded-up South Chicago Chapel funeral home is seen from the bedroom window of James Kinney, a decades-long resident of South Deering who lives near the South Chicago Chapel funeral home, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/752769f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6280x3524+0+476/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F11%2Fff26614d42989f7645a8d130843b%2Ffuneralhomesmell-260814-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f486f38/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6280x3524+0+476/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F11%2Fff26614d42989f7645a8d130843b%2Ffuneralhomesmell-260814-6.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/752769f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6280x3524+0+476/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F11%2Fff26614d42989f7645a8d130843b%2Ffuneralhomesmell-260814-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The boarded-up South Chicago Chapel funeral home is seen on Aug. 12 from the bedroom window of James Kinney, a decades-long resident of South Deering who lives near the funeral home.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In 2016, after multiple years of denied access to the building, the city took the building owners at the time, Midwest Group of Illinois, to court. Initially, the city raised the possibility of a receivership for the property, or demolishing it altogether, according to court records.</p><p>But the case was eventually dismissed after owners achieved “substantial compliance” with the city’s orders. The building failed six more inspections in the years that followed. A representative for Midwest Group told WBEZ/Sun-Times the property was “mostly vacant” for several years leading up to its sale in 2023.</p><p>It was sold to an entity managed by Clark Morgan, and property tax bills haven’t been paid since 2024, according to the Cook County treasurer’s office.</p><p>Ferguson said the building’s troubled history should have indicated a need for more attention, even after a change in ownership.</p><p>“At least an initial inspection — post-turnover of ownership — would have signified this is a carryover of an unacceptably long-term, non-compliance situation,” he said. “You would have wished somewhere in those three or four years there had been some form of inspection.”</p><p>But Ferguson pointed to a broader problem of understaffing and “unfunded mandates” citywide that he said are out of the building department’s control.</p><p>“The fact of the matter is they don't have the resources they need, and what happens is, quite often, signals are overlooked, and it results in situations like this,” he said.</p><p>On Friday, the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/08/31/clark-johanna-morgan-south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-lawsuit-building-department" > city filed a housing complaint </a>in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging 23 different code violations at the property discovered during the August search, including the failure to keep the building “clean, sanitary, and safe.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Run-ins with regulators, tax collectors and suburban police</b></h3><p>Clark Morgan got a state license as a funeral director and embalmer intern in 1997, the year before his wife got her director and embalmer license. Under state law, interns are allowed to handle bodies under the supervision of a director/embalmer, who are also broadly authorized to “engage others who are not licensed.”</p><p>They both had their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/10/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-oversight-illinois-decomposing-bodies" target="_blank" ><u>licenses suspended</u></a> in 2017 after failing to file state income taxes. Johanna Morgan was also reprimanded and fined $1,500 that year for transporting “a decedent across state lines for burial prior to obtaining required permits,” Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR) records show.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Revenue has issued four tax liens on their Evergreen Park home since then, most recently earlier this year with more than $14,000 owed to the state.</p><p>Clark Morgan let his intern’s license expire in 2019 and then had it revoked completely in March 2024, a tumultuous year for the couple.</p><p>After IDFPR officials discovered Clark Morgan removed “at least two” bodies from Northwestern Memorial Hospital using a license with “an altered expiration date,” he was fined $10,000 and agreed to stop “engaging in the practice of funeral directing” in Illinois.</p><p>Johanna Morgan was fined $5,000 in the same month in 2024 for failing to complete and file three death records “in a timely manner” in 2020.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2f0000" name="image-2f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The home of Clark and Johanna Morgan in Evergreen Park, on Aug. 7, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>A previous grisly discovery</b></h3><p>Then in the overnight hours of June 13, 2024, an Evergreen Park police officer on patrol near the couple’s home in the 9400 block of South Avers stopped to check Clark Morgan’s minivan, which was double-parked, according to a report from the suburban police department.</p><p>The officer found two bodies inside and “a strong odor of what appeared to be rotting meat from within the vehicle,” the officer reported.</p><p>The couple came outside, with Clark explaining he had picked the bodies up from hospice care for cremation at their Chicago Heights crematory and “stopped at his house to go to the bathroom and grab something to drink quickly,” according to the police report.</p><p>Johanna Morgan “was not cooperative with me and advised she didn`t think it was suspicious to have deceased bodies in the back of a van because her and her husband are funeral directors,” the officer reported.</p><p>Johanna showed police “dispatch messages regarding a pickup” but told officers “she did not want to give out personal information of the deceased,” the report said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/28/sisters-mothers-cremated-remains-south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home" >Sisters have doubts about cremated remains: ‘Where is my mama?’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>After the officers pulled up the Morgans’ state license information online and perused Illinois’ funeral directing law, Johanna and her husband “were released from the scene to continue their work,” police said.</p><p>Officers followed up the next day with the Cook County medical examiner’s office, where an investigator said he had “filed numerous complaints against Heights Crematory for unprofessional practices” but explained hospice cases don’t go to the medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Johanna provided the names of the two dead individuals from the back of the van in a phone call with an officer the next day, and a hospice nurse told police she referred the person’s family to Planet Green Cremations, the report says, another venture of the Morgans.</p><p>Evergreen Park police closed the case after checking with the Cook County state’s attorney’s office, where a prosecutor said the case did “not meet any criminal requirements.”</p><p>“Clark did not go out of his way to stop at home as his home address is on the way from both residences. Johanna has an active license as a funeral director and embalmer. Therefore Clark can transport under the general supervision of a licensee that need not be immediate to a crematory,” the report said.</p><h3><b>Crematory shutdown</b></h3><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" target="_blank" ><u>different set of regulators</u></a> zeroed in on the couple the next year, when IDFPR received a February 2025 complaint about the Morgans’ operation at Heights Crematory. The agency referred the complaint to the Illinois comptroller’s office, which, in <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/investigations/2026/08/18/south-deering-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-illinois-lax-oversight-inspections" target="_blank" ><u>a quirk of state law</u></a>, oversees crematories and cemeteries, while IDFPR regulates funeral directors.</p><p>Comptroller’s office investigators shut down the facility after finding dozens of bodies piled upon each other “in varying stages of decomposition, mummification, and not being stored in proper alternative containers,” records show.</p><p>At least 44 bodies were mishandled at Heights Crematory along with 504 sets of cremated remains, authorities said. As of mid-August, the medical examiner’s office was still trying to locate the families of 454 deceased people from the Chicago Heights case.</p><p>The episode prompted IDFPR officials to visit locations affiliated with the Morgans — including South Chicago Chapel in March 2025, “to investigate for potential unauthorized funeral directing activities,” according to Gov. JB Pritzker’s office.</p><p>Comptroller Susana Mendoza revoked Heights Crematory’s license in June 2025, but the Morgans admitted no wrongdoing as part of their consent order with the state.</p><p>Mendoza’s office “urged IDFPR to take away Johanna Morgan’s funeral license” due to the crematory’s troubling conditions, and referred the case to the state’s attorney’s office and the Illinois State Police to investigate potential criminal charges.</p><p>Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke’s office “recommended that ISP continue its investigation and consider the possibility of financial crimes,” according to a spokesperson. ISP officials earlier this month said their investigation was ongoing.</p><p>IDFPR officials visited South Chicago Chapel again Oct. 7, 2025, according to a timeline provided by Pritzker’s office.</p><p>“No serious concerns pertaining to the handling or storing of remains,” were identified, according to the governor’s office, but IDFPR filed formal disciplinary charges against Johanna Morgan three days later seeking permanent license revocation.</p><p>Agency officials wouldn’t say what prompted that visit or the charges, citing the ongoing disciplinary case that preceded the horrific discovery at South Chicago Chapel this August.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" flags before 56 decomposing bodies found at South Chicago Chapel</h2><br><ul id="rte-57108ac2-a573-11f1-8c0a-5f1979675e3d"><li>City building inspectors didn’t do an annual inspection at 2939 E. 95th St. for the past four years.</li><li>The building itself had a history of failed inspections, which one expert says should have prompted greater attention</li><li>Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation reprimanded Clark and Johanna Morgan repeatedly from 2017-25.</li><li>Evergreen Park police found two bodies in the Morgans’ van on their residential block in 2024.</li><li>Illinois Department of Revenue issued four liens on their home from 2022-26.</li><li>Property tax bills were delinquent at 2939 E. 95th St. for the past two years.</li><li>Illinois comptroller’s office shut down their Chicago Heights crematory for mishandling of bodies in 2025.</li></ul><br></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Heir to a revolutionary past, playwright and author Zayd Ayers Dohrn charts his own path
entries.summary: <p>In May 2024, when Northwestern University made a deal with pro-Palestinian student protesters to dismantle their encampment, Fox News headlined its story this way: “Northwestern professor, whose school gave in to anti-Israel agitators, is son of notorious terrorist radicals.”</p><p>Even when Zayd Ayers Dohrn is secluded in his ivory tower along the shores of Lake Michigan and minding his own business, he can’t escape the taint of his parents’ revolutionary past.</p><p>“I of course had nothing to do with that deal and nothing to do with the protests,” said Dohrn, a playwright, screenwriter and the aforementioned Northwestern academic.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In his memoir, “Dangerous, Dirty, Violent, & Young,” published in May 2026, Zayd Ayers Dohrn recounts his childhood as the son of Weather Underground revolutionaries and the family’s life as fugitives. Bill Ayers (left), Zayd Dohrn and Bernardine Dohrn walk outside federal court in New York in 1982. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provides; AP Photo/David Handschuh</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dohrn, 49, has come to accept as “inevitable” that anyone writing about him will dust off the exploits of his parents, Bill Ayers and Bernardine Dohrn, leaders of the Weather Underground, a militant leftist group that went to war with the U.S. government in the 1960s and early ’70s. His mother was at one point on the FBI’s “Ten Most Wanted” list.</p><p>But despite his mother’s hopes that he would follow in her revolutionary footsteps, he became a writer and an academic who still struggles with how his parents were willing to risk everything — including tearing the family apart — to fulfill their radical ambitions. He lays bare those feelings in “Dangerous, Dirty, Violent, & Young,” Dohrn’s memoir about his parents and the family’s life as fugitives, published earlier this year in May.</p><p>The book comes on the heels of “Revolution(s),” Dohrn’s first musical and a collaboration with Rage Against the Machine’s Tom Morello, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2025/10/02/revolutions-goodman-theatre-tom-morello-musical-zayd-ayers-dohrn" target="_blank" ><u>premiered</u></a> at the Goodman Theatre last year.</p><p>Dohrn calls America’s wealth gap “grotesque,” but his liberal worldview is less rigid than that of his parents, often in surprising ways.</p><p>Campus “trigger warnings” and “safe spaces” are well-meaning concepts that went too far, said Dohrn, who is tall and angular but also bears a striking resemblance to his mother.</p><p>“Then it was institutionalized, and now kids get indoctrinated by deans giving orientations about safe spaces and they react against that,” Dohrn said, calling such orientations “ridiculous.” “My students find it deeply patronizing and absurd.”</p><p>Dohrn explores his ambivalence toward so-called hate speech on university campuses in his new play, “The Humanities,” which opens Sept. 13 at Victory Gardens Theater, and deals with the fallout after a controversial speaker is invited to lecture at an elite university.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“The play is in miniature sort of a metaphor for the country, as represented by the university as a place of competing identities that are struggling to form this more perfect union and divided against itself in so many ways,” Dohrn said.</p><p>While you can imagine a young Bernardine Dohrn heckling (or worse) Luka Jarry, the fictional right-wing provocateur invited to the play’s fictional Lincoln University, Dohrn sees shades of gray.</p><p>“I could get better crowds elsewhere. A higher honorarium anywhere… But this is more important. To me. To all of us. Because where else do people care so much? You know? I mean where else are people so ready? To be changed?” Jarry says shortly after he arrives on campus.</p><p>Said Dohrn: “Generally speaking, my feeling is that you meet hate speech with more speech, and we have to find a way to have a healthy enough civic discourse that we can allow bad people to say bad ideas and then combat them in the kind of sphere of intellectual discourse.”</p><p>Does that mean sometimes giving protesters the boot?</p><p>“If they disrupt the speech to the point where it’s impossible to hear, you have to,” he said.</p><h3>A childhood among radical outlaws</h3><p>Our conversation shifts to Dohrn’s parents and his book about their revolutionary lives, a fascinating and also deeply disturbing read.</p><p>Before he was 5 years old, Dohrn — thanks to his dad’s instruction — knew how to instantly spot danger.</p><p>“A Black guy and a white guy rolling by together, in Harlem? In 1981? Unless they’re Gene Wilder and Richard Pryor, they’re probably cops,” Dohrn writes of his early childhood on the East Coast.</p><p>Dohrn’s parents never wasted an opportunity to try to mold their son’s young mind.</p><p>“When I begged for a G.I. Joe action figure for my birthday, [Dohrn’s father] tried to explain to me that G.I. Joe was a recruitment tool for the U.S. military, a symbol of American imperialism and macho gun violence — the embodiment of everything our family was fighting against. I didn’t care,” Dohrn writes.</p><p>Dohrn returns often to the subject of the peril he and his younger brother, Malik, faced simply by being in the back seat of the car with their outlaw parents, whose campaign against the U.S. government included blowing up buildings (remarkably, no one but three of their own Weather Underground accomplices were killed).</p><div class="Enhancement" destroying his family.</p><p>“Every f___ing minute,” replies Bill Ayers. “Every minute. I am 76 years old, and I have felt the most vivid sense of having survived and squeaked through again and again and again.”</p><p>But Dohrn said that as a child, he never felt unloved or neglected.</p><p>“In a larger sense, their goal was to make the world a better place for me. It’s complicated, but I don’t see them as selfish, neglectful, abusive, cruel,” he said.</p><p>Ayers, now 81, is retired, after a career as a professor in the University of Illinois-Chicago’s education department. Bernardine Dohrn, 84, is a retired Northwestern University law professor. They live in Hyde Park. She has been diagnosed with dementia, her son said, but was still able to read Dohrn’s book and watch his plays.</p><p>Dohrn and his novelist wife, Rachel DeWoskin, have two grown children of their own, daughters. One is studying journalism in college; the other is in design school. Neither of them grew up on the run.</p><p>“Our family dinners, the conversations are … more about art and less about politics, but they are still intense conversations about the state of the world … and what is each of our obligation to the future,” Dohrn said.</p><p>As a parent, Dohrn said he was far less “doctrinaire” than his own parents, although he said he and his wife have raised their kids with a similar sense of “racial and gender justice.”</p><p>But how would he feel if his family’s radical tendencies resurfaced in, say, a vote for a high-profile Republican?</p><p>“That would be difficult,” Dohrn said, chuckling. “Of course we want our kids to be free thinkers, we want them to be happy, we want them to find lives that they feel are charged with meaning.”</p>

entries.title: Skylar Diggins out for remainder of Sky's 2026 season
entries.summary: <p>No surprise here: Skylar Diggins is out for the remainder of the 2026 season, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> announced Tuesday.</p><p>The Sky were eliminated from the playoffs and have only four games remaining, leaving little incentive for the veteran guard to return.</p><p>The Sky’s statement said that they want to “prioritize Skylar’s long-term health after collaboration and communication with Skylar and her team, Sky doctors, and the organization’s medical staff.”</p><p>Diggins had not played since early July, when she posted on Instagram about being moved to the bench. Coach Tyler Marsh described it as a “coach’s decision.”</p><p>Diggins <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/06/skylar-diggins-caught-off-guard-by-benching-as-tension-builds-with-sky" >expressed disappointment</a> about the communication and resources from the organization, and said then that she had been playing through knee pain resulting from a procedure in October.</p><p>“I’ve been sacrificing my body for this team,” she said. “Maybe it’s time to take a step back and see what’s going on to see if I need to continue to make those sacrifices without having the proper resources to play at an elite level.”</p><p>Diggins has been rehabbing the injury ever since. She also said more recently that she’d had productive conversations with Marsh and wanted to contribute to winning basketball.</p><p>“We’re in full support of Skylar and want to make sure we are steadfastly prioritizing her health,” general manager Jeff Pagliocca said. “Skylar made a strong effort to get back to the court this season. She’s been in constant communication with us through the entire process.”</p><p>Diggins is signed to an $1.86 million deal through 2027.</p>

Woelfel</a></h5><p><b>Troubled history</b>: The tax bills piled up for years on Clark and Johanna Morgan, the Evergreen Park couple who ran a network of crematory and funeral services across the South Side and suburbs. So did a series of professional disciplinary cases, along with a bizarre run-in with police who found two bodies in the back of a minivan outside their home. And that was before authorities discovered dozens of mishandled corpses at the Morgans' now-shuttered Chicago Heights crematory.</p><p><b>Warning signs disregarded</b>: No apparent red flags proved enough to prevent another gruesome discovery this summer: 56 unrefrigerated, decomposing bodies inside the couple's South Chicago Chapel, a building that had its own troubled history with city inspectors long before the Morgans acquired it.</p><p><b>City sues</b>: The city of Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydmjko-l-o/" target="_blank" >is taking the responsible?</b>: Our review of public records underscores the tangled web of oversight responsibilities across multiple levels of government that officials are grappling with to prevent another collaboration between county prosecutors and federal immigration agencies across Illinois during the first 15 months of President Donald Trump's second term.</p><p><b>Data share</b>: State's attorneys daughters, ‘loved everybody’</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydmjko-l-a/" target="_blank" >David Struett</a>, <a class="Link" Chen</a></h5><p><b>Celebration turns deadly</b>: On Saturday night, a reunion in Washington Park among former Robert Taylor Homes residents ended in tragedy when masked gunmen opened fire, killing Rontonio Guterz and wounding 14 other people in the largest mass shooting in Chicago this year.</p><p><b>Family in mourning</b>: Guterz, 35, was the youngest of 12 siblings and was known among family as "Tray," according to his sister. Guterz had a girlfriend and three young daughters, and he'd just bought a truck after earning his commercial driver's license, his sister told the Sun-Times. "He was such an outgoing person," she said. "He loved everybody."</p><p><b>Search for answers</b>: Local Ald. >CPS seeks to make it easier for students experiencing homelessness to enroll, get support</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydmjko-l-ji/" target="_blank" >Emmanuel Camarillo</a></h5><p><b>Policy change</b>: For the first time in a decade, Chicago Public Schools is changing how it serves students experiencing homelessness and youth without legal guardians, aiming to make it easier for them to enroll in school and access support.</p><p><b>What's new</b>: Under the new policy, approved unanimously by the Chicago School Board, students in temporary living situations must be enrolled the same day they present themselves at the school zoned for where they are staying. The changes also require schools to dedicate private spaces where students can seek help.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: At least 22,000 CPS students — about 6.8% — experienced homelessness during the 2024-2025 school year, according to the Chicago Coalition to End Homelessness. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydmjko-l-il/" target="_blank" >Somer Van Benton</a></h5><p>For organizers of Chicago’s Black & Bronze Festival, Saturday's event in Bronzeville was intended to gather and connect neighbors from different generations in Armstrong Park.</p><p>They wanted the Bronzeville fest, now in its second year, to recreate the feeling of the traditional front porch — a place where generations naturally crossed paths, where children learned from elders, neighbors looked out for one another and stories moved from one generation to the next.</p><p>"Where Grandma and the grandbabies and aunts and uncles and cousins were all together," founder Jessica La Rel told WBEZ.</p><p>One way that connection was forged among the hundreds who attended Saturday was live jazz music, food, panel discussions, dance performances and more.</p><p>"I think Bronzeville — the broader South Side — can be disparaged in a way where people think that only crime, poverty, a lack of investment or care in the community exist," La Rel said. entries.title: Paul Kahan, Manny’s Cafeteria & Delicatessen garner top 2027 Banchet honors
entries.summary: <p>Chef Paul Kahan will receive the 2027 Culinary Excellence Award, and Manny’s Cafeteria & Delicatessen will receive the 2027 Iconic Restaurant Award at the 25th Banchet Awards, the city’s top food honors, in January.</p><p>The awards are named in honor of Jean Banchet, the legendary chef who ran Wheeling’s Le Francais restaurant in the 1970s and ’80s, helping to raise Chicago’s culinary profile.</p><p>Kahan, partner and executive chef of One Off Hospitality Group, which includes Avec, The Publican, Big Star and Dove’s Luncheonette, said in a statement he’s “grateful to have entries.title: Summer of 2026 wasn't total loss — at least there are tomatoes
entries.summary: <p>Did your tomatoes come in this year? Yes? A bountiful crop? That's too bad, because wastewater from cooling the giant AI data centers being built all over the country has gotten into the national aquifer, and the flesh of tomatoes is particular adept at soaking up microplastics and neurotoxins. Best to let them rot on the vine this year, or better yet, dig a pit and bury them, just to be safe.</p><p>Kidding. None of the above is true — there is no such thing as a "national aquifer" — though at this point it feels like anything is possible, in the bad news department, after a summer of serial tornadoes, massive wildfires and nightmare glacier-melt flash floods blasting mountain towns. Plus wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine and probably a few places I'm forgetting. </p><p>Meanwhile the same ongoing opera buffa plays out in Washington, where paying attention to any specific jaw dropper — wait, he told a <i>lie</i>? — seems an act of raw naivete. I wouldn't be surprised if the president declared a crazy trade war with our good friend Canada, slapping it with a 50% tariff that it would immediately slap back on us, then rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" in a fit of toddler pique that had people all over the world shaking their heads in a blend of amusement, pity and disgust.</p><p>Oh wait, that really happened.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Back to tomatoes. Records are spotty, but for the past five years it's been a sorry sight at my place — hard little green spheres of shame that never ripen. To make matters worse, it's been a perpetual tomato-palooza over at my brother's house. He would meet me for lunch with a grin and a shopping bag filled with ripe red beauties, any one of which would have made my season. I tried to convince myself that he merely stops at a farmers market and loads up, just to stick it to me the way only a little brother can. But I know his wife is tending the garden back home, so I cannot suggest deception.</p><p>"What's Japanese for 'tomato shame'?" I asked. My sister-in-law is from Osaka.</p><p><i>"Tomato no haji,</i>" he said.</p><p>I distracted myself by focusing on the Japanese word for tomato — <i>tomato</i> — which seems odd, since the fruit came to that country in the 1600s with Portuguese traders. So how did Japanese tomatoes end up tagged to an English loan word name? The short answer is: They didn't. Both Japan and the United States borrowed the word from the same source. Tomatoes are thought to have originated in South America, probably Ecuador or Peru, then found their way to the future Mexico, where the Aztecs named them <i>tomatl</i> — kind of cool that, magically transported to Tenochtitlan in 1400 and hungry after a morning building pyramids, you could ask for a fresh tomato and have a reasonable expectation of getting one.</p><p>I hung my head in profound <i>tomato no haji</i>, accepted my brother's gift, and vowed to do better.</p><p>And this year I did do better. How? I bought a fancy pH meter — my wife felt that, given the results, the soil must be poisoned — but could never make it work, so took it back. Maybe just the act of trying could, in some quantum observer effect way, have changed the tomato dynamic. Plus dosing the plants with Miracle Grow Plant Food.</p><p>Maybe because I had rotator cuff surgery July 22, so couldn't really tend to the garden in any way for the next month, taking me out of the equation might have helped. Plus, my brother gave me half a dozen of the cherry tomato plants that grow in his garden like weeds, and those came through, big time. Though, given the last time my tomatoes really took off was the first COVID summer of 2020, I'm open to the idea that tomatoes show up when you need them most.</p><p>We've been eating them like mad. Bright red circles of tomato on thick slices of Kaufman's challah, slathered with butter. Cherry tomatoes tossed into salads by the handful — they can also be popped in the mouth, one at a time, like candy. My wife roasted tomatoes, with onions and peppers, into a sauce over tilapia.</p><p>And the joy of giving them away. My neighbor brought over a mason jar of homemade cream of red pepper soup and a French bread as an act of charity for the infirm. I returned the jar filled with cherry tomatoes.</p><p>And Friday I'm taking my brother out for his annual birthday lunch. But the real treat will be when I hand over, with a flourish, a small container of tomatoes, trying to ignore what I imagine will be the brimming shopping bag on the chair next to him.</p>

entries.title: Standoff ends with arrests at Kenwood home
entries.summary: <p>Two people were led away in handcuffs after an apparent SWAT situation ended Tuesday afternoon in Kenwood. </p><p>The incident happened in the 4300 block of South Lake Park Avenue, according to Chicago Fire Department spokesperson Larry Merritt. </p><p>No injuries have been reported. </p><p>As of early afternoon, a Sun-Times photographer witnessed two people being led away in handcuffs. Officers were leaving the scene. </p><p>Chicago police had no further information immediately available. </p><p><i>This is a developing story. entries.title: La sensación térmica podría superar los 100 grados esta semana, dicen los meteorólogos
entries.summary: <p>Algunas partes del área de Chicago podrían sentirse más calientes de los 100 grados esta semana, ya que una ola de calor afecta la zona, dicen los pronosticadores.</p><p>Es probable que la propia ciudad de Chicago se libre del índice de calor más intenso —o de cómo se siente la temperatura— de casi 105 grados Fahrenheit, que se espera que alcance los suburbios del sur el martes y el miércoles.</p><p>En cambio, en Chicago las temperaturas podrían subir a los 80 el martes y a los bajos 90 el miércoles, según Zachary Yack, meteorólogo de la oficina del Servicio Meteorológico Nacional en Romeoville. El lunes, el máximo fue de 87 grados en Chicago, según el servicio meteorológico.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6b0000" name="module-6b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" entries.title: GM Ryan Poles: I don't know if Kyler Gordon will play for Bears again
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> general manager Ryan Poles can't guarantee cornerback Kyler Gordon will play for the team again. </p><p>"I don't know," he said Tuesday. "I would hope so. I still have hope there. He's going to have to continue to work hard to get back to playing football."</p><p>It was the latest twist in the bizarre case of Gordon's calf injury, which kept him out of most offseason activities and all of training camp. He was put on the physically unable to perform list at the start of training camp and remained there when the team <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/30/bears-transaction-tracker-cut-day-decisions-ryan-poles-ben-johnson-gervon-dexter-ryan-poles-nfl" target="_blank" >made cuts Sunday</a>, meaning he has to miss at least the first four games of the season.</p><p>Gordon has been rehabbing with Bears trainers — and, like most players, has outside help, too. Poles was asked whether there was a disconnect between what pain Gordon has told the team he's feeling as opposed to the Bears' assessment of his injury.</p><p>"Any time you have an injury and you're coming back from something, there's a discomfort you have to push through," he said. "And that's what it comes down to. We haven't been able to get over that hump and we're not progressing as fast as we'd like to."</p><p>Still, it's not hard to read between the lines. </p><p>Tuesday, Poles said the other two players on PUP, linebacker Noah Sewell and defensive lineman Shemar Turner, were "doing a really good job with our performance team" and that they were "fired up to start that clock and get going."</p><p>His next sentence?</p><p>“And then Kyler is on that list as well," he said. "We'll see when he comes back. I don't have a timetable. We'll see how that goes."</p><p>He then went on to praise the Bears' trainers and rehab support staff.</p><p>Poles said in late July that there was a "delay" in Gordon's recovery after he spent the team's summer break doing rehab at Halas Hall. He said then that it was "all hands on deck to get him back" and that there was frustration from both Gordon's side and that of the team. That's been apparent whenever coach Ben Johnson is asked about Gordon — he's given curt answers, usually saying that he had no update.</p><p>In most circumstances, a coach would offer platitudes about how the player has rehabbing intently or how excited the team would be to get him back. Instead, these are the full answers Johnson has given about Gordon in the last month or so.</p><p>When asked about his status Aug. 18, Johnson said "there's nothing to add right now."</p><p>Asked about it Aug. 15, Johnson replied with one word: "Unknown."</p><p>On Aug. 6: "There's no update. Just continue to rehab."</p><p>Gordon traveled with the team to Cincinnati for their joint practice and exhibition game but did not go to Nashville last week. </p><p>The Bears signed Gordon to a three-year, $40 million extension in April 2025. Cutting him outright during this season seems unlikely — it would cause Gordon's $12.91 cap hit for 2026 to rise by about $10 million. The Bears have only a $5 million dead cap charge if they cut him next year.</p><p>The Bears were excited about his presence — in coordinator Dennis Allen's opening press conference, Gordon was the only player he mentioned by name. </p><p>Gordon, though, struggled through a series of injuries last year, at first early in training camp and then, bizarrely, when he was added to the injury report on an off day before the season opener. He returned in October, got hurt the following week, and returned again in November before getting hurt in warmups before the Bears' rivalry game in Green Bay. He was dynamic in the playoffs, though, providing a glimpse of what the Bears paid so handsomely for. </p><p>He played in only three regular-season games, though, and started only one.</p><p>"This spring was going to be a springboard for us to get going the right direction," Johnson said in June.</p><p>It never happened.</p>
