entries.title: La administración de Trump anuncia operativo contra escuelas de manejo de camiones comerciales
entries.summary: <p>Dos oficinas de fiscales federales del interior de Illinois se sumaron el lunes al Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos para anunciar una ofensiva contra las escuelas de entrenamiento para conductores de camiones que, según la administración de Trump, han ayudado a inmigrantes sin documentación a obtener licencias comerciales de conductor (CDL).</p><p>Las autoridades federales cerraron 110 escuelas de manejo de CDL en todo el país vinculadas con más de 5,000 conductores "que no aprobaron las pruebas de dominio del inglés", según el Departamento de Justicia.</p><p>Otras 160 escuelas fueron clausuradas tras inspecciones que detectaron supuestas instalaciones inadecuadas y algunos instructores sin licencia.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ce0000" name="module-ce0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>No quedó claro cuántas estaban en Illinois. Pero las oficinas de dos fiscales federales de Illinois —Steven Weinhoeft, del Distrito Sur, y Greg Gilmore, del Distrito Central— fueron nombradas en una amplia fuerza de tarea encargada de auditar escuelas adicionales.</p><p>El gobierno federal establece los estándares de las pruebas para las CDL, mientras que los estados emiten las licencias. Un portavoz del Secretario de Estado de Illinois, Alexi Giannoulias, dijo que su oficina cumple con las normativas nacionales y no tenía comentarios sobre la nueva iniciativa.</p><p>Un portavoz del gobernador JB Pritzker, crítico abierto de Trump, afirmó que la administración "está optando por atacar a los camioneros por cómo lucen o por cómo hablan".</p><p>"La administración de Trump está usando excusas para invalidar cientos de escuelas de entrenamiento que no hacen nuestras carreteras más seguras —solo están atacando a nuestra esencial fuerza laboral de camioneros y a las cadenas de suministro mientras la nación enfrenta una escasez nacional de conductores de camión", dijo la oficina de Pritzker.</p><p>La ley federal exige que los titulares y solicitantes de CDL "muestren prueba de presencia legal y domicilio".</p><p>En Illinois, las pruebas se administran únicamente en inglés, una disposición impulsada hace casi tres décadas tras un escándalo de licencias por sobornos que contribuyó a la caída del difunto exgobernador de Illinois, George Ryan, condenado a nivel federal.</p><p>La fuerza de tarea federal se produce tras un intento de la administración de Trump de obtener acceso a bases de datos con información sensible sobre miles de titulares de CDL en todo el país, una medida que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/08/14/administracion-de-trump-exige-a-illinois-y-otros-estados-datos-sensibles-de-conductores-de-licencias-cdl" target="_blank" >el fiscal general de Illinois, Kwame Raoul, ha demandado para bloquear</a> junto con los principales fiscales de otros 20 estados.</p><p>La administración ha amenazado con recortar más de $10 millones en fondos federales a la American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators por no entregar los últimos cinco años de datos del sistema Commercial Driver’s License Information System.</p><p>La base de datos fue creada a finales de la década de 1980 para ayudar a los estados a determinar la elegibilidad de los conductores para las CDL entre distintos estados.</p><p>Raoul y otros fiscales generales sostienen que la administración de Trump está violando tanto la ley estatal como la federal al crear su propia versión de la base de datos sin salvaguardas para el manejo de información sensible, como los números de Seguro Social.</p><p>Las demandas afirman que la administración "no tiene una necesidad legítima de apoderarse de esta base de datos de registros estatales, y no consultó a los estados antes de hacer este cambio drástico".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bears practice report: 'Week 0' starts with reshuffled roster
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the Bears’ first practice of “Week Zero” on Tuesday:</p><h3><b>What happened</b></h3><p>The Bears practiced mostly special teams during a practice that lasted a little over an hour.</p><h3>Why the trade?</h3><p>Bears GM Ryan Poles said “timing and fit” were the reason he decided to trade defensive tackle Gervon Dexter to the Falcons for cornerback Clark Phillips III and a fifth-round pick. He also praised rookies Jordan van den Berg and Jayden Loving, whose emergence gave him the flexibility to make the trade.</p><p>Poles liked Phillips’ man coverage skills. He’s played mostly outside cornerback in the NFL after playing the slot in college. The Bears are likely to use him at the former.</p><h3><b>Roster moves</b></h3><p>The Bears signed defensive lineman James Lynch and linebacker Jack Sanborn to the active roster to replace safety Coby Bryant and tight end Hayden Large, who went on injured reserve.</p><p>They added 14 practice-squad players: running backs Salvon Ahmed and Zavier Scott; offensive linemen Caden Barnett, Kyle Hergel and Christian Jones; receivers Kaden Davis, Scotty Miller and J.P. Richardson; tight end Stephen Carlson; defensive lineman Marcus Davenport; linebacker Buddy Johnson and Wayne Matthews III; and defensive backs Deantre Prince and Marlen Sewell.</p><h3>Injury update</h3><p>Only three players on the 53-man roster didn’t participate Tuesday: running back Kyle Monangai, linebacker D’Marco Jackson and defensive end Austin Booker. Poles said he wasn’t sure if Booker, who has a groin injury, will be ready for Week 1.</p><h3></h3><h3><b>What’s next</b></h3><p>The Bears will practice Wednesday, focusing on situational football, before holding a padded practice Thursday.</p>

entries.title: Ciudad de Chicago ofrece subvenciones de $10,000 para apoyar el acceso a alimentos en los lados sur y oeste
entries.summary: <p>Negocios pequeños y mercados de agricultores pueden recibir subvenciones únicas mediante un nuevo programa municipal creado para ampliar el acceso a los alimentos.</p><p>El Programa de Subvenciones para Mercados de Vecindario proporcionará hasta $10,000 a negocios pequeños que operen en áreas con poco acceso a alimentos, según un comunicado de prensa difundido el viernes.</p><p>El anuncio del programa se produce un mes después del cierre abrupto de siete tiendas Save A Lot en los lados sur y oeste de la ciudad. El operador, Yellow Banana, tenía un acuerdo de construcción con la Ciudad para mantener los locales abiertos durante 10 años.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-440000" name="module-440000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"El acceso a alimentos frescos y saludables no debería depender del barrio en el que vives", dijo Johnson en el comunicado de prensa. "El Programa de Subvenciones para Mercados de Vecindario destina recursos directamente a los negocios pequeños y a los operadores de mercados que están ayudando a cambiar eso —fortaleciendo los sistemas alimentarios locales, apoyando a emprendedores del vecindario y ampliando el acceso a alimentos frescos en todo Chicago”.</p><p>Según la Ciudad, pueden postular dueños de negocios minoristas pequeños y de alimentos y bebidas, así como operadores de mercados de agricultores que tengan una localidad en "geografías prioritarias".</p><p>Los fondos pueden usarse para la compra de equipos, la operación de mercados, la promoción y divulgación, y mejoras para mantener los mercados abiertos durante todo el año.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/sites/bacp-recovery-plan/home/neighborhoodmarketgrantprogram.html" target="_blank" >Las solicitudes</a> se aceptarán hasta el 25 de septiembre a las 5 p.m. Las solicitudes en español estarán disponibles a partir del miércoles.</p><p>El programa está financiado por el Plan Road to Recovery de Chicago, y Allies for Community Business aportó $450,000 al programa para los beneficiarios de las subvenciones.</p><p>A principios de este mes, Johnson también anunció otro programa para ayudar a mejorar el acceso a alimentos tras el cierre de Save A Lot. La Ciudad tiene una asociación con Lyft, United Way of Metro Chicago y 211 Metro Chicago para otorgar a personas mayores en los lados sur y oeste hasta <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2026/august/senior-grocery-rides.html" target="_blank" >dos créditos de Lyft de $25</a> para ayudarles a llegar a los supermercados.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Chicagoan dies of West Nile virus
entries.summary: <p>A Chicagoan has died from West Nile, and is among the first two human cases this year, the city's department of health announced Tuesday.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health has also confirmed <a class="Link" href="https://click.citynews.chicago.gov/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5ODZ9AAoAAAAABFAGA5vqmku_wt80yYdbVlWvrJxn0c6P6c7XpNj7ZiyHqxcLpg9Ozws_EUPMtStyu_QSl1zsDV4e_-tupmdohZ7_ekX08A3DpXKapQ" target="_blank" >several additional cases</a> of the virus in the state of Illinois.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Public Health did not identify the person who died. </p><p>"2026 has seen the rainiest summer in Chicago in years, giving mosquitoes ample opportunities to breed," city Public Health Commissioner Garth Walker said in a statement. "The best way to protect yourself from West Nile virus is to avoid mosquito bites and take measures to stop them from breeding around your home."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">News Announcement: 📢 CDPH Confirms Chicago's First Human Cases, One Death from West Nile Virus in 2026<br><br>Read the full release at <a href="https://t.co/SDiyYfOyUk">https://t.co/SDiyYfOyUk</a><br><br>For more information about mosquito levels in Chicago and mosquito-borne diseases, visit <a href="https://t.co/j7W0KkHau4">https://t.co/j7W0KkHau4</a>. <a href="https://t.co/AwOEc1YhM8">pic.twitter.com/AwOEc1YhM8</a></p>— CDPH | Chicago Department of Public Health (@ChiPublicHealth) <a href="https://x.com/ChiPublicHealth/status/2094858008660492491?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 1, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/28/suburban-cook-county-reports-first-4-west-nile-virus-cases-of-2026" target="_blank" >Late last month, the Cook County Department of Public Health reported</a> the first four cases of West Nile virus in suburban Cook County this year and urged residents to take precautions against mosquito bites.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i><br></p>

entries.title: Trump says Chicagoans 'will die' without his help, as Pritzker, Johnson blame him for anti-violence cuts
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Mayor Brandon Johnson are pushing back on President Donald Trump's critique of Chicago's "unchecked" levels of violence — instead blaming the president for gutting anti-violence programs.</p><p>The latest back and forth between the political rivals happened early Tuesday when the president wrote on Truth Social that "Chicago violence is unchecked and at record levels." Trump's comments came after a weekend <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/31/washington-park-mass-shooting-chicago" target="_blank" >mass shooting in Washington Park</a> left one man dead and 14 others injured. </p><p>"These numbers are becoming normalized. It is out of control! The city will die if the Federal Government, a fine tuned crime fighting machine, is not invited in, by the Mayor or Governor, to HELP," Trump wrote. "I am awaiting the call. Nobody should be forced to live under these conditions. Like D.C. and others, they will have almost no crime, FAST! The State and City can’t do what I do. Governor Pritzker, CALL!!!"</p><p>Trump employed similar language during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/28/trumps-blitz-on-chicago-targeting-the-worst-of-the-worst-only-detained-five-murderers-in-68-days" target="_blank" >“Operation Midway Blitz”</a> when he said both Johnson and Pritzker should have asked him for help with crime in the city, and amid massive protests against immigration enforcement. The enforcement led to a protracted legal battle over use of the National Guard, which the president ultimately lost. Pritzker and Johnson instead put up a unified front against Trump's targeted operation in Chicago, which left <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/05/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-trump-silverio-villegas-gonzalez" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas-Gonzalez</a> dead and injured <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/25/marimar-martinez-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-chicago-police-cpd" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez.</a></p><p>“When Trump last sent agents to Illinois, they murdered a father and shot an innocent woman in broad daylight — then attempted to cover it up," Pritzker said in a statement. "We need to keep reducing violence, but this President does not make it easier. If only he hadn’t defunded the very programs that help.”</p><p>The governor's office on Tuesday also accused Trump of "enabling" crime — not fighting it. </p><p>"Governor JB Pritzker would like to set the record straight: this is the same federal administration that launched a lawless, lethal invasion on Illinois and gutted funding for gun violence prevention in the U.S.," his office said. "Trump is not fighting crime — he is committing and enabling it."</p><p>The Department of Justice last year cut more than $800 million in federal grants nationwide for violence prevention and public safety programs, citing shifting goals at the agency. </p><p>Johnson on Tuesday defended the city's investments in driving down violence in Chicago, noting that last year marked the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/01/chicago-crime-murder-homicide-shooting-president-trump-mayor-johnson" target="_blank" >fewest homicides since 1965.</a></p><p>"The president of the United States of America has an open invitation to invest in the people of Chicago, and we've called for these investments repeatedly. He removed over $800 million out of gun violence reduction programs. He cut the ATF budget by 30%," Johnson said at a press conference. "You know when you have a president who is literally defunding the operations that can actually assist us in creating safer communities, it's difficult to take anything that he says seriously."</p><p>The mayor called Trump a "sorry individual." </p><p>"If he was serious about driving violence down, not just in Chicago but across the country, he would not be engaged in endless illegal wars. The president is investing more to bomb children than he is to feed children," Johnson said. "He has an open invitation in Chicago and across this country to reverse the largest upward transfer of wealth that he placed into the hands of the ultra-rich, and actually fund the institutions and operations that ultimately provide safety and security for the people of this city and this nation."</p><p><i>Contributing: Mariah Woelfel</i></p>

entries.title: Jim Ruddle, Chicago TV news anchor who sailed into the sunset, dies at 94
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Jim Ruddle made his mark on Chicago as a respected broadcast newsman who, quite literally, sailed into the sunset after his last broadcast.</p><p>He had a reputation as an old-school professional who could skillfully craft a news script in minutes and, utilizing a photographic memory, recite it by heart on air.</p><p>He arrived in Chicago in 1965 and worked at WGN-TV (Channel 9) before taking a position at NBC-owned WMAQ-TV (Channel 5). He later worked at WTTW-TV (Channel 11) alongside the late John Callaway and served as a network correspondent for NBC News before returning to NBC 5 as a news anchor and nightly commentator.</p><p>"There's an art form to great reporting and writing, and Ruddle was a master of both," said former NBC 5 colleague Carol Marin.</p><p>"He knew how to ask really hard but fair questions, and he respected the people he interviewed but he didn't pander to them and he wasn't coy."</p><p>"He liked smart, no-bull---- people because that's who he was and what he was," Marin said. "He also had strong opinions and could offer eviscerating commentaries, but he knew what he was talking about."</p><p>Mr. Ruddle retired in 1986, boarded his sailboat, named Zarzuela, and sailed to the Bahamas. He lived on his boat and sailed the islands for several months. He later sailed around the United States.</p><p>"He said 'I'm not working holidays, or any other days!' and he decided to go follow his dream," said his son, Blake Ruddle.</p><p>Mr. Ruddle died Aug. 27 in Rye, New York, from natural causes. He was 94.</p><p>"He retired on his own terms; he was coming up for contract, and he'd won Chicago Emmy Awards and a Peabody Award, and he was just fed up with the economics and politics that became more and more a part of the news, which he felt had essentially turned from journalism into show business," said his son.</p><p>In 1988, during his post-retirement sailing adventure, he told the Chicago Tribune, “I’ve nothing to go back to. I sit in that cockpit and talk to myself and give my views and opinions and thoughts on very serious subjects. And, of course, no one is listening. It’s just like talking to a news director.”</p><p>Mr. Ruddle began his career in his hometown of Tulsa in an era when the news he read went on radio and television broadcasts simultaneously.</p><p>When he was a network correspondent for NBC News, his job took him many places.</p><p>In 1978 he went to Rome to cover the papal conclave that resulted in the election of Pope John Paul II. Weeks later he found himself in freezing Northwest Canada after a Soviet spy satellite with a nuclear reactor malfunctioned and crashed back to earth.</p><p>For many years, Mr. Ruddle, who lived in Hyde Park and later Glenview, enjoyed a drink and a song.</p><p>"He and I liked to go into taverns once in a while, and we both liked to sing old songs, like songs from Johnny Mercer and Cole Porter," recalled his former NBC 5 colleague Peter Nolan. "And sometimes a barkeep would come up and say 'Pete, I'll give you ten bucks if you and Ruddle won't sing tonight,' but most of the time they liked it."</p><p>In his retirement, he wrote a children's adventure novel titled "My Name is Luke" about a boy in 1858 New England who falls asleep on his grandfather’s schooner and is kidnapped by two seafaring villains.</p><p>Mr. Ruddle was born during the Great Depression on May 20, 1932, in Tulsa to George and Lucille Ruddle. He was a lawyer. She was a homemaker.</p><p>Mr. Ruddle served in U.S. Coast Guard and attended the University of Tulsa.</p><p>"He was not a conspicuous guy. He wore a pair of blue jeans, and wore them until he wore them out, and then got another pair of blue jeans," his son said.</p><p>In recent years, as the necessary maneuvering on the deck of a sail boat became difficult, he maintained his love for the sea by purchasing an old fishing boat that he used to cruise the Long Island Sound.</p><p>Mr. Ruddle, was preceded in death by his wife, Anne. He's survived by daughters Emily Ruddle, Brey Sloan, Kristen Ruddle, and son Blake Ruddle, along with six grandchildren and five great-grandchildren.</p><p>"He loved the news. Whatever came in that day, he always wanted to be a part of it," said his longtime companion Marilyn Balamaci, a magazine reporter and editor. "Fundamentally, being a journalist was in his blood."</p><p>A celebration of life that will take place in Chicago is being planned.<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago's top cop says Washington Park mass shooting was ‘somewhat targeted,’ likely involved gunfight
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s acting top cop told reporters Tuesday that police think a mass shooting at a gathering in Washington Park over the weekend was “somewhat targeted” and likely involved multiple shooters and an exchange of gunfire.</p><p>As city officials announced the opening of a resource center for those impacted by violence, interim police Supt. Fred Waller also alluded to the potential use of a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/10/11/machine-guns-handguns-switches-sears-extended-capacity-magazines-tommy-gun-larry-snelling-al-capone" > “switch,”</a> a small device that turns a semi-automatic pistol into a machine gun.</p><p>“It happens in a matter of seconds, but we also know that there probably was some return fire also, so some people in the crowd [were] probably armed,” Waller said, standing alongside Mayor Brandon Johnson and other city leaders at the Washington Park Refectory.</p><p>The shooting happened around 11:30 p.m. Saturday as former residents of the Robert Taylor Homes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/30/mass-shooting-kills-1-injures-9-large-gathering-washington-park" target="_blank" >gathered for a reunion</a> on the east edge of the park in the 5400 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue, according to police and a victim of the attack.</p><p>Chicago Park District Supt. Carlos Ramirez-Rosa said the police were “working to close the park and disperse individuals” when the gunfire began about half an hour after the park was supposed to close.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/31/washington-park-mass-shooting-chicago" target="_blank" >Rontonio Guterz, 35, was killed</a>, and 14 others were wounded in Chicago’s largest mass shooting this year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-000000" name="image-000000"></a> says two gunmen wearing ski masks opened fire, and someone at the gathering shot back.</p><p>At least 36 shell casings were found on Cottage Grove Avenue and inside the park, including casings from a rifle, according to the report. A weapon was also recovered.</p><p>Waller told reporters the number of casings could indicate there was “more than just one offender.” He said investigators have obtained “some videos tracking vehicles” and were “canvassing the scene” for all types of footage.</p><p>Ald. Jeanette Taylor (20th) told reporters she drove past the park around 8 p.m. and thought about reporting the cars she saw parked on the grass. But she said she knows the “effects of calling the police prematurely, so I didn’t call.</p><p>“They were just out there hanging, listening to music. They were eating. You saw kids out there, like it was a good time. My only beef was: Get off the grass," Taylor said. "And so hindsight being 20/20. People should be able to hang out at the park. That's not the issue. The issue is when you got some idiot who decides to go up and shoot in a crowd.”</p><p>Johnson said the shooting was “absolutely unacceptable, and it does not reflect the true nature of who we are as Chicagoans.</p><p>“In the face of that pain, our responsibility is not simply to condemn what happened,” the mayor said. “It is to show up for the people who are harmed, surround this community with support, and then make sure that no one has to navigate the aftermath of this tragedy alone.”</p><p>Mental health services, crisis support and help applying for victim compensation will be available at the fieldhouse from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. Thursday.</p><p>Waller said the department’s victim services team is canvassing the area Tuesday to spread word about the event, which is open to the public regardless of whether someone was involved in the most recent shooting.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/30/mass-shooting-kills-1-injures-9-large-gathering-washington-park" target="_blank" >Chicago’s biggest mass shooting this year sees 1 killed, 14 hurt in Washington Park</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/31/washington-park-mass-shooting-chicago" target="_blank" >Man killed in Chicago’s largest mass shooting of 2026 was outgoing, ‘loved everybody,’ his sister says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 'Goofy' is gone as Bears coach Ben Johnson sees sharper focus from QB Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> mentioned throughout training camp how much he liked quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>’ businesslike approach to practices, and that’s a big step from where he was going into their first season together.</p><p>Johnson said before practice Tuesday that Williams has been a total pro this summer.</p><p>“I've seen a very composed person every time he steps into the building,” he said. “This guy might’ve had a little bit of goofy to him a year ago, and I use that term with love. Now you just see a more serious player and intent every time I'm around him. His teammates feel that as well.</p><p>“He's getting to the practice field early. He's making sure his part is taken care of. He's warmed up, he's ready to go. He stays after with the guys. You guys see that on a regular basis. He's taking a lot of pride in his approach right now, and it trickles down to everyone around him. It's a great thing. He continues to grow up and he's going to be a huge leader for us this year.</p><p>For context, Johnson clarified that by “goofy,” he meant that last year there were times Williams would “get sidetracked or distracted a little bit,” but this summer, “That has not been the case.”</p><p>Williams and Johnson are going into their second season together, and Williams’ third since the team drafted him first overall. He made strides under Johnson last season, but still has significant steps to take when the Bears open the season Sept. 13 at the Panthers.</p>

entries.title: White Sox officially add Tommy Pham and Tanner McDougal to active roster, DFA Tyler Gilbert
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/tyler-schweitzer-tyler-gilbert-white-sox-davis-martin-will-venable-kyle-teel-ryan-fuller-astros-series-houston" target="_blank" ><u>Tommy Pham’s second stint with the White Sox</u></a> has officially begun, which requires official moves in response.</p><p>While Pham and hard-throwing right-hander Tanner McDougal were added to the active roster on Tuesday as part of MLB rosters expanding to 28 players on Sept. 1, the White Sox also had a full 40-man roster. One day after being optioned to Triple-A, left-hander Tyler Gilbert was designated for assignment to make room for Pham’s addition.</p><p>After posting a 3.88 ERA in 51 innings for the Sox last season, occasionally working as an opener, the 32-year-old Gilbert has thrown just six major league innings this year and allowed eight earned runs. Gilbert missed over a month of action with shoulder impingement, and has spent the bulk of the year in Triple-A while lefties Chris Murphy and Tyler Schweitzer have gotten more big league run.</p><p>As essentially the second right-handed platoon bat on the roster behind Randal Grichuk, the 38-year-old Pham is filling a niche role for the final month of the White Sox’ playoff hunt. But the Sox anticipate his presence offering more than that of the typical part-time player.</p><p>“The human being, the teammate, the edge that he brings, kind of who he is as a total player, I think he’s going to make a real big impact here,” said Sox manager Will Venable. “He’s honest, convicted in what he believes in. He’s just a good player that’s really smart and super professional.”</p><p>McDougal made his major league debut on Aug. 13, and it quickly went sideways. In his first outing in almost two weeks, he walked three batters and hit another to push a run across in a 9-8 loss to the Reds, and was optioned to Triple-A after the game. The results weren’t much better upon McDougal’s return to Charlotte, as he walked six and allowed three homers in 4⅔ innings over five appearances.</p><p>In general, McDougal’s midseason conversion to relief after missing two months for a flexor strain has been wonky. But the Sox believe the talent and stuff that made McDougal a preseason top-100 prospect per <i>Baseball America</i>, and saw him run a 3.00 ERA with 27 strikeouts in 24 innings in the first month of entries.title: Aspira to let judge decide what happens to money from sale of taxpayer-funded school, following WBEZ report
entries.summary: <p>After Aspira of Illinois declared bankruptcy in June, the nonprofit listed a building constructed with $27 million in taxpayer funds that housed one of its closed charter schools. In court records, the nonprofit indicated that it planned to use money from the sale to pay off debt and continue operating with whatever was left.</p><p>But last week, an attorney for the nonprofit told a judge that Aspira will, instead, put money from the sale aside and wait on the court to decide where it should go. Exactly how much money Aspira could walk away with is unclear: Chicago Public Schools sent an attorney to the hearing on the sale of the property, indicating that the school district is ready to make a case that it should get some, if not all, of the remaining money.</p><p>These latest developments in Aspira’s bankruptcy case come after <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/08/11/former-charter-school-operator-aspira-declares-bankruptcy-could-profit-from-sale-of-taxpayer-funded-building" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times published an article</u></a> questioning whether Aspira could pocket money from the sale. What happens in this case could set a precedent for what happens to assets purchased with public funds when private operators close charter schools in Illinois. CPS has been criticized for not going after the assets of closed charters in the past, but it appears the district is stepping in now.</p><p>CPS officials said in a statement issued Friday that they “refrain from providing details on pending legal proceedings” but noted that they are working through “appropriate legal proceedings to ensure that any and all property and assets purchased with public funds are returned to the District.”</p><p>A lawyer and officials with Aspira did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Aspira of Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/05/aspira-will-soon-have-no-teachers-or-money-cps-is-still-struggling-to-close-it" target="_blank" ><u>ran into financial trouble in March</u></a> and was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/19/cps-revokes-aspiras-ability-to-operate-charter-schools-in-chicago-in-rare-move-board-of-education" target="_blank" ><u>forced to close down two charter schools</u></a> in Avondale on the city’s Northwest Side. More than 500 students <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/02/26/cps-to-shut-down-financially-distressed-aspira-campuses-scattering-students-to-new-schools" target="_blank" ><u>had to find new places to learn midyear</u></a>. And Aspira’s modern school at the intersection of Milwaukee and Monticello avenues was left empty.</p><p>Aspira filed for bankruptcy in June and then about a month later asked the court to allow it to sell the state-of-the-art building for $11 million.</p><p>Aspira officials explained in court documents that the money would be used to pay off a $5.8 million mortgage on a smaller, older building, as well as about $1.5 million of debt to a number of creditors, including the Chicago Teachers Pension Fund.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>When Aspira put its former high school up for sale, the listing touted that the building remained in pristine condition.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Aspira officials also indicated in court records that they planned to use the rest of the money to continue operating in some capacity. The organization still runs an alternative school that’s funded through CPS and Aspira’s interim executive director said in a statement last month that, going forward, the organization is focused on “rebuilding and rebranding.”</p><p>CPS’ claim to some of the proceeds from the sale likely stems from its contract with Aspira, which stated that if the nonprofit ceased to operate its schools, the organization “shall” return “any property or assets” purchased with CPS funds that were used to run its schools.</p><p>State law seeks to clear up any ambiguity by saying that anything “purchased with public funds shall be returned to the school district” from which the charter drew its enrollment.</p><p>Though the state footed the bill to construct the building that’s up for sale, state officials have not responded to questions about whether they will go after the proceeds, nor have their attorneys showed up in court.</p><p>Reporting by WBEZ and the Sun-Times seems to have altered how the proceeds will be handled.</p><p>When Aspira’s attorney, Paul Bach, got in front of the judge last week seeking approval for the sale, he noted he spoke with CPS’ attorney after a “news article that everyone has read” was published, referring to an August report by WBEZ and the Sun-Times.</p><p>He said Aspira proposed a plan in which it would pay off some of its debts and put roughly $4 million into an escrow account, which the organization cannot access until the judge decides what should be done with it.</p><p>Bach also touched on the question of whether $11 million is a fair price for a former school building that cost $27 million in state funds to build. When Aspira put the Milwaukee Avenue building up for sale, <a class="Link" href="https://images1.showcase.com/d2/RutaJhL163YxVze3jesqELgIqTH9LQRuJ30-mKM00F4/document.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>the real estate listing touted</u></a> that it remains in pristine condition, and has had “significant capital investment” that would “support continued use or seamless adaptive reuse.”</p><p>Bach told the court that $11 million was “by far the best offer we have received to date” and the next closest offer was $7 million.</p><p>He implored the judge not to put off the sale. “The whole idea is to get this property sold,” he said last week, pointing out that each month Aspira has to keep paying the mortgage on its second building is “detrimental,” as it eats into how much money the organization has on hand.</p><p>An attorney for the Chicago Teachers Pension Fund asked Aspira to agree to a financial audit. Charter schools are supposed to cover some of their staff’s retirement benefits. According to court documents, Aspira owes the pension fund more than $200,000.</p>

entries.title: As hitters rack up ‘insane’ home-run totals, Jed Hoyer needs more consistent pitching for Cubs to ‘fare well’
entries.summary: <p>On the first day of the regular season’s final month, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> president Jed Hoyer was able to talk with confidence about his hitters.</p><p>That’s easy to do on the heels of a record-setting home-run derby.</p><p>The Cubs established a new franchise mark with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/31/cubs-brewers-jed-hoyer-trades-free-agency-alex-bregman-clay-holmes-tyrone-taylor" >nine homers in Monday night’s win</a> over the Brewers, also leaping into the major league record books by finishing August with 62 dingers, the second-highest single-month total ever.</p><p>“To hit 62 homers in a month is insane,” righty pitcher Kevin Gausman said Tuesday.</p><p>The Cubs started September as baseball’s best offensive team, leading the sport with 742 runs scored, 196 homers and a .341 on-base percentage.</p><p>They started the month still seven games back of the Brewers in the NL Central standings, but they look like one of baseball’s true championship contenders.</p><p>“One through 9, they’re coming at you,” Gausman said. “And they’re hard to gameplan against.</p><p>“There’s not too many holes. When I think about a lineup, I think about pockets where, ‘If I can get these two guys out, it kind of sets up the rest to where I can maneuver this lineup.’ This lineup doesn’t really have that.”</p><p>But Hoyer wasn’t exactly all smiles Tuesday, his confidence in the bats and gloves not exactly matched by his thoughts on the pitching — and recent results.</p><p>While the Cubs’ scalding hot bats finished August with a bang, the team came into September having dropped four of their previous five series.</p><p>“We’ve been really streaky, which has put us in a good position, but obviously, we’ve had some series recently where we’ve struggled,” Hoyer said. “We’ve got to play well consistently. That’s what has my attention the most. We’ve done that for large periods of the season. This late-August period wasn’t our strongest.</p><p>“The position-playing group, we’re the No. 1 offense, No. 1 defense right now. That’s wonderful. Obviously, that’s the backbone of our team. … There’s no question of what our strength is. We do need to get consistent starting pitching, throw strikes consistently and hopefully let the position players do the work.”</p><p>Those comments obviously come at a moment in time.</p><p>Lefty starter Shota Imanaga has had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/30/chicago-cubs-shota-imanaga-three-homers-cincinnati-reds-craig-counsell-jody-davis-jon-lester-ed-howard-edward-cabrera" >back-to-back clunkers</a> and leads the sport with 33 home runs allowed, bringing to mind his late-season struggles a year ago.</p><p>Lefty Matthew Boyd was strong last week against the Diamondbacks but still finished August with a 5.23 ERA in five starts, a stumble following a stretch in which he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/25/chicago-cubs-game-1-playoff-starter-matthew-boyd-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-shota-imanaga" >looked like a Game 1 playoff starter</a>.</p><p>And a bullpen that had been mostly solid this summer has been knocked around of late, with righty closer Jacob Webb <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-walk-off-loss-diamondbacks-clay-holmes-kevin-gausman-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-bullpen" >serving up walk-off homers in consecutive outings</a> on the recent road trip and relievers allowing nine runs in a pair of losses to the Reds last weekend.</p><p>Not knowing what you’re going to get is a problem come playoff time, when one sour outing could mean an early start to the offseason.</p><p>While Cubs bats led the sport in homers as September started, Cubs pitchers led the league in the same category, with 209 long balls allowed.</p><p>“We’ve given up a lot of homers. Obviously, that’s something we’ve got to work on is giving up fewer homers,” Hoyer said. “The home-run ball has been a challenge for us, and it’s something that, not only this year but going forward, we have to really think through.</p><p>“When the ball’s in play, we have the best chance of any team to catch it. But we can’t do much if the ball goes in the seats.”</p><p>That’s not to say the outlook is dire, as Hoyer’s trade-deadline work has been a smashing success to this point. Gausman and fellow righty Clay Holmes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/19/cubs-clay-holmes-kevin-gausman-jed-hoyer-trade-deadline-tyrone-taylor-playoffs" >have been mostly great since being acquired</a>, and Hoyer described them as “stabilizing forces” for the pitching staff.</p><p>Hoyer can maybe add those two to the list of what he can count on, along with his team’s position players.</p><p>But the arms, in general, need to be better more often if the Cubs are going to be the last team standing.</p><p>“We’re just trying to get to a point where if we can get consistent starts,” Hoyer said, “we know with our position-playing group, our offense, that we’ll fare well.”</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: Create the perfect bite with spicy shrimp with sweet corn salsa
entries.summary: <p>Salsas are much more than red or green sauces for dipping chips. Taking a cue from the spicy Latin dance that shares the name, edible salsas are a party of ingredients that collide and crunch in your mouth, bursting with sweet, spicy, tangy flavors that brighten up anything they accompany, including meats, fish, vegetables and, of course, chips.</p><p>Each ingredient plays a role in creating a bright and lively salsa. The key is to gather a tasty, colorful team that provides a fiesta of colors, flavors and textures. Fruit, vegetables, fresh herbs, even beans are all fair game. The variations are endless, but like certain dance steps, there are a few rules of thumb to follow to create the perfect bite.</p><p>Keep the pieces small to ensure that every ingredient is in each bite. Cut and dice the ingredients in uniform size. Aim for a variety of textures, including juicy, crisp, soft and leafy. Embrace the color — after all, we eat with our eyes, too. Choose ingredients that not only pop in your mouth but also stand out on the plate.</p><p>Most important, check the flavor boxes with a combination of sweet, salt, acid and heat. Sweetness can be in the form of vegetables or fruit, such as corn, red bell peppers, carrots, pineapple, stone fruit or mangoes. Tart is best achieved with acidic ingredients, such as a squeeze of citrus or a splash of vinegar. Depending on what kind of you, tomatoes can bring sweetness or acidity. Heat is delivered by chiles, hot sauce or an abundance of freshly ground black pepper. And remember to taste, taste, taste as you build the salsa.</p><h3>Spicy Shrimp With Sweet Corn Salsa</h3><p><b>Active time:</b> 30 minutes<br><b>Total time:</b> 30 minutes<br><b>Yield:</b> Serves 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Salsa</b><br>Corn kernels from 2 ears of corn (or 2 cups defrosted frozen corn)<br>2 to 3 scallions, white and green parts divided, thinly sliced<br>1 medium red bell pepper, seeded, finely diced<br>1 medium orange bell pepper, seeded, finely diced<br>1 jalapeno pepper, seeded, finely chopped<br>1 garlic clove, grated<br>1/4 cup Italian parsley leaves, chopped<br>1/4 cup cilantro leaves and tender stems, chopped<br>1 tablespoon fresh lime juice<br>1 tablespoon fresh orange juice<br>1/2 teaspoon ground cumin<br>1/2 teaspoon kosher salt, or to taste<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or to taste</p><p><b>Shrimp</b><br>1 teaspoon sweet paprika<br>1 teaspoon smoked paprika<br>1 teaspoon ground cumin<br>1 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper<br>1 pound large (18/20) shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails intact (optional)<br>2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil<br>Fresh cilantro leaves for garnish<br>Lime wedges for serving</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Place the salsa ingredients in a bowl. Stir to combine and taste for seasoning.</p><p>In a small bowl, combine the paprikas, cumin, salt, black pepper and cayenne and stir to blend.</p><p>Place the shrimp in a large bowl. Add the oil and toss to coat. Sprinkle the spices over the shrimp and toss again to evenly coat.</p><p>Heat a cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Arrange the shrimp in one layer in the pan without overcrowding. Cook until bright pink in color and just cooked through the centers, about 4 minutes, turning once. Transfer to a plate.</p><p>Spoon the salsa on serving plates. Arrange the shrimp over and around the salsa. Garnish with chopped cilantro and serve with lime wedges.</p>
entries.author: Lynda Balslev

entries.title: Try this simple no-cook tomato sauce to beat peak summer heat
entries.summary: <p>When tomatoes are at their peak — and it's too hot to turn on the oven — this simple, no-cook sauce from my cookbook "Pasta Every Day" is what I come back to time and again. It's often called pomodoro crudo and served with very thin spaghetti, though you'll find many variations, including those with onions, capers, olives and local cheese.</p><p>In that spirit, don't hesitate to make this your own.</p><p>You can use any flavorful tomato here, from heirloom to plum to cherry. Remove the skins and seeds of the larger varieties if you'd like, or keep it rustic and leave them intact (I prefer the latter). The pasta will soak up the garlicky tomato juices over time, meaning it makes for great (dare I say better?) leftovers and picnic fare.</p><h3>No-Cook Tomato & Basil Sauce</h3><p>Serves 4 (enough for about 22 ounces of fresh pasta or 16 ounces of dried pasta)</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p>2¼ pounds ripe, small tomatoes<br>4 garlic cloves, finely chopped<br>1½ loosely packed cups fresh basil leaves, roughly torn, plus more for serving<br>Kosher salt<br>1/3 to 1/2 cup high quality extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for serving<br>Finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano or Pecorino Romano, for serving (optional)</p><p>Directions<br>Prepare the sauce: Halve or quarter the tomatoes and combine with the garlic and basil in a large serving bowl. Season generously with salt, then drizzle in the oil. Stir to combine. Leave the sauce to sit, covered, for at least 1 hour, ideally in a warm, sunny place.</p><p>Cook your pasta of choice to your liking — this is not a time for undercooking and finishing in the sauce. Add the pasta to the sauce and stir to combine. Finish with another drizzle of oil, more basil and a shower of cheese if you'd like. If you can bear it, let the pasta marinate in the sauce for 15 minutes before serving.</p><p><b>Tip</b><br>If using larger tomatoes, I often peel and seed them before chopping. To do so, bring a pot of water to a boil and fill a large bowl with ice water. With a paring knife, score the bottoms of the tomatoes with a small X, just piercing the skin. Drop them into the water and cook until the skin near the X starts to loosen, about 2 minutes. Use a slotted spoon to transfer them to the ice bath. When the tomatoes are cool, peel away the skins. Remove the pulp and seeds and roughly chop the flesh.<br>___</p><p><i>Meryl Feinstein is a chef, pasta maker and food writer. She founded Pasta Social Club and lives in Washington, D.C., where she teaches pasta-making workshops. She was the Resident Pasta Maker on the online site Food52.</i></p><p><i>Excerpted from "Pasta Every Day" by Meryl Feinstein. Copyright (copyright) 2023 by Meryl Feinstein. Used with permission of Voracious, an imprint of Little, Brown and Company. New York, NY. All rights reserved.</i></p>

entries.title: Vibrant salad inspired by Italian panzanella takes advantage of sweet corn and juicy tomatoes at their peak
entries.summary: <p>Nothing says summer like a brimming bowl filled with fresh garden vegetables and farmers market finds. Sweet corn and juicy tomatoes are at their peak, which makes for a perfect pairing in this vibrant salad inspired by Italian panzanella.</p><p>Panzanella is a rustic bread-and-tomato salad from Tuscany and Umbria. Traditionally, stale bread is softened by the juices of salted ripe tomatoes, then tossed with a simple vinaigrette. This version isn't strictly traditional, but it captures the spirit of the classic. Grilled croutons add toasty flavor and texture, while ripe tomatoes, crisp fresh corn, quick-pickled red onions and a bright basil vinaigrette bring everything together.</p><p>Once the components are prepped, the salad is easily assembled. Start with the basil dressing, which is thicker than a classic vinaigrette (add a splash more olive oil if you prefer a lighter consistency). Give the red onions a quick soak to mellow their bite and enhance their natural sweetness. Grill or toast the bread until crisp and lightly charred. And for the corn, keep it raw if it's fresh and in season. The kernels are crisp and juicy, with a naturally sweet and milky flavor that shines in the salad.</p><h3>Tomato and Corn Panzanella Salad</h3><p><b>Active time:</b> 20 minutes<br><b>Total time:</b> 40 minutes<br><b>Yield:</b> 4 to 6 servings</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Dressing</b><br>2 cups fresh basil leaves<br>1 garlic clove, chopped<br>2 tablespoons red wine vinegar<br>1/4 teaspoon kosher salt, or to taste<br>1/8 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil</p><p><b>Salad</b><br>1/2 medium red onion, thinly sliced<br>2 to 3 tablespoons red wine vinegar<br>1/2 French or Italian baguette<br>Extra-virgin olive oil<br>Kosher salt<br>4 ounces arugula (or assorted mixed greens)<br>Kernels from two ears of yellow or bicolor corn<br>6 medium ripe tomatoes (about 1 pound), such as Early Girl or heirloom, cut into bite-sized chunks or wedges</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Combine all the dressing ingredients, except the oil, in the bowl of a food processor. Pulse to chop. Add the oil and pulse to blend. The dressing should have a salsa consistency. If you prefer it runnier, add more oil to your taste. Transfer to a bowl and cover with plastic wrap to prevent discoloring.</p><p>Place the onion in a small bowl. Sprinkle the vinegar over and stir to coat. Let stand for about 20 minutes. Drain and blot dry with a kitchen towel.</p><p>Cut the baguette in half lengthwise. Brush the cut sides with oil and lightly season with salt. Grill or broil until golden and charred in spots, turning once, 3 to 4 minutes. Remove and cool to the touch, then tear into bite-sized pieces.</p><p>Combine the arugula, corn, tomatoes, onion and bread in a wide serving bowl. Drizzle with some of the dressing and gently toss to combine. Serve with more dressing to your taste.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i><br></p>
entries.author: Lynda Balslev

entries.title: Tony Romo pleads no contest to operating while intoxicated
entries.summary: <p>CBS NFL analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo has pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated and has issued a statement apologizing for the actions that led to his July arrest.</p><p>Romo was arrested July 23 following a traffic stop as he was driving south on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin. CBS has since placed him on leave from his role as its lead NFL analyst.</p><p>According to Milwaukee County court records, Romo lost his driving privileges for six months and was ordered to complete an alcohol assessment program.</p><p>Romo also owes $834. An interlock device must be installed on any vehicle owned or operated by Romo or registered to his name, and that order will remain in effect for at least one year after he is issued a license.</p><p>"The past month has been difficult, but it has also been personally significant," Romo said in a statement on Instagram. "It has required me to confront and own my mistakes fully — to the Lord, to myself, to my family and now to the public."</p><p>Romo said the multiple back surgeries that led to his retirement as a player "left me with constant, debilitating pain." He noted that the pain "led to a dependence on pain medication, and my efforts to get off those medications led to an over-reliance on alcohol."</p><p>"None of this is an excuse," Romo said. "These are my failures and I take responsibility for them."</p><p>Romo said he is working with a team of doctors to address his health and "make the necessary changes." He thanked his family, friends and the NFL community for their support.</p><p>"As I turn my attention to my health, my family, and, in time, my return to CBS, I kindly ask for privacy during this period," Romo said.</p><p>Romo also initially had received citations for possessing open intoxicants in a motor vehicle, unsafe passing on the right and refusal to take a test for intoxication after arrest. Those citations have all been dismissed.</p><p>CBS Sports president David Berson said last month that he does not have a timeline for a decision about Romo's future with the network.</p><p>Romo, 46, has been the lead game analyst for CBS' NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a playing career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.</p><p>Analyst JJ Watt will join play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on CBS Sports' lead NFL team during Romo's absence. Their first game will be on Sept. 13, when the Minnesota Vikings host the Green Bay Packers.</p><p>Citations released by the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office indicated that Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests and that an open bottle of an alcoholic beverage was found in the passenger's side of his black Jeep during an inventory before it was towed.</p><p>Body camera footage showed Romo telling deputies he had been coming from a golf course and was on his way "to visit grandma and grandpa" when he was stopped. A deputy told Romo he suspected him of being impaired because he had "red glassy eyes" and an "odor of an intoxicating alcoholic beverage."</p><p>Romo went to high school about 35 miles southwest of Milwaukee in Burlington, Wisconsin.</p><p>He remains the Cowboys' franchise leader in career touchdown passes with 248. He held the franchise record for career passing yards (34,183) until Dak Prescott overtook him last season.<br></p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Skylar Diggins leaves her future with the Sky open to interpretation
entries.summary: <p>Mark Skylar Diggins down as a “we’ll see” for 2027.</p><p>After a rocky first season in Chicago for the veteran point guard — one that is ending early, with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> announcing she will miss the remainder of the season to continue rehabbing her knee — Diggins left her intentions for next year open to interpretation.</p><p>On paper, she still believes the Sky have a playoff roster. If not for the injuries and the team’s struggles in close games, she suggested, their preseason vision might have borne out.</p><p>But when asked about her future with the Sky, her comments were difficult to parse.</p><p>“The decision that I made and that we made as far as … shutting it down for this season has nothing to do with next year, in my opinion," she said.</p><p>“We’ll just have to see how this offseason goes. But we’ve never had any talks with the organization about trades or wanting a trade or anything like that during this process.”</p><p>She continued: “Whatever happens in this free agency — or not free agency — in this next year and whatever goings-on, I haven’t expressed any desire to not talk about me in a Chicago Sky jersey next year.”</p><p>Very well then!</p><p>Once upon a time, Diggins was the Sky’s splashiest free-agent acquisition — if a curious one, given that they already had another future Hall of Fame point guard in Courtney Vandersloot.</p><p>On Tuesday, she said the decision to shut her down this season was made to protect her health and future with the organization.</p><p>But speaking to reporters for 20 minutes in an early exit interview, Diggins never offered what you hope for from a star setting: a resounding vote of confidence in the franchise's direction.</p><p>She reiterated that her biggest frustration this season was the lack of a practice facility. The Sky had promised theirs would be ready by the start of the season but instead bounced among local college gyms. Diggins said that limited her recovery from knee surgery she underwent in October.</p><p>It also didn't sound as though she had gained much confidence in head coach Tyler Marsh.</p><p>Marsh benched Diggins in early July, prompting a social media post in which she questioned the decision. She later questioned his end-of-game management <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/07/skylar-diggins-and-tyler-marsh-still-not-aligned-after-benching" >in an interview with the Sun-Times.</a></p><p>When asked Tuesday whether Marsh was the right person to lead the organization into the future, she called it a “great question” that she would love to reflect on.</p><p>There’s good reason for Diggins to be ambivalent about Marsh. Though he improved significantly in his second season, the team still underperformed and repeatedly faltered in close games.</p><p>But there’s reason for the organization to be ambivalent about Diggins, too.</p><p>She was the Sky’s leading scorer in 19 games, but her finishing at the rim declined significantly, especially in clutch situations — the same moments that so often doomed the team.</p><p>Maybe the knee injury explains it. Diggins said she did not feel like herself this season and was limited by her health from the get-go. But perhaps it reflected a genuine decline in her play or a fundamental lack of fit.</p><p>Both sides now need to spend the offseason reflecting on whether their shared vision still makes sense.</p><p>Do the Sky really want to run back an experiment built around multiple accomplished veteran point guards and an inexperienced coach? Does Diggins?</p><p>These are questions everyone involved might have considered more carefully last winter.</p><p>We’ll see whether they reflect more thoroughly this time around.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: CTA lacked 'meaningful security' when man was fatally stabbed on Blue Line train in January, lawsuit says
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Transit Authority failed to keep a man safe when he was fatally stabbed on a Blue Line train earlier this year, a new lawsuit alleges. </p><p>Dominique Pollion, 37, had fallen asleep on the train early in the morning Jan. 10. Around 2:15 a.m., a man entered the train — holding a knife and recording with his phone — and stabbed him in his chest and abdomen. Pollion awoke, screamed and tried to escape his attacker, but he collapsed on the floor of the train car, according to security footage referenced in the complaint. Pollion was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where he was pronounced dead. </p><p>A lawsuit filed Monday in Cook County court on behalf of Pollion's grandmother alleges the CTA and its private security officers failed to respond until the train arrived at the Clark and Lake station. And as first responders tried to revive Pollion, the security guards stood by as his attacker stuck around and continued recording Pollion, according to the suit. He then was able to leave the scene without being detained. </p><p>After the incident, Chicago police used security footage to identify Pollion's alleged attacker, 40-year-old Demetrius Thurman, who was arrested two days later and charged with first-degree murder. Detectives found a video on Thurman's phone of the fatal stabbing and other photos of sleeping CTA passengers, according to the lawsuit. He remains in jail until trial.</p><p>"Dominique Pollion never should have been alone with that man on the train in the first place," Michael Cerasa, the lawyer with Romanucci & Blandin representing Pollion's grandmother, said during a Tuesday news conference. "This case is ... about a system of oversight and protection that failed Dominique Pollion at every single point where it had a chance to save his life." </p><p>The suit also names Thurman and two of the CTA's private security contractors, Monterrey Security and Action K-9 Security. The CTA abruptly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/04/20/cta-private-security-guard-contract" target="_blank" >ended its multimillion dollar contract</a> with Monterrey in April. Last year, Action K-9 was awarded an $89 million, two-year contract. </p><p>A representative for Monterrey Security declined to comment because the company has not been formally served the complaint. However, its records show that the company did not have guards patrolling the Blue Line or the Clark and Lake station when Pollion was killed.</p><p>A CTA spokesperson declined to comment on pending litigation. A representative for Action K-9 Security did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Pollion's grandmother, Shirley Pollion-Hines, spoke Tuesday about her grandson's compassion and the dreams he had to improve his and his family's life.</p><p>"It would be easy for Dominique's life to be just reduced to a statistic, or simply a horrible tragedy and a waste," she said. "But you need to know that his life was bigger than how he died. There were people who knew his smile, heard his laughter and watched him grow up."</p><p>At the time Pollion was killed, "the CTA had a long and documented history of violent crime occurring on their system," Cerasa said. "They did not ever take the most basic steps to have meaningful security on the system." </p><p>Violent crime on public transit has fallen dramatically this year after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/10/chicago-transit-authority-cta-crime-security-plan-fta" target="_blank" >CTA bolstered security</a> on trains, buses and platforms. That security surge came after a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/19/president-trump-chicago-cta-crime-security-funding-cut-mayor-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >funding cut threat</a> from the Trump administration and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/02/chicago-cta-transit-crime-assault-battery-leerhsen" target="_blank" >a Chicago Sun-Times investigation</a> that found aggravated assaults and batteries on the CTA reached at least a 24-year high in 2025. </p><p>Last month, Action K-9 Security <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/07/action-k9-security-cta-red-line-fare-evasion" target="_blank" >was sued after its security guards</a> stood by as a fare evader knocked over a woman entering the 95th Street Red Line station. </p><p>Read the lawsuit here: </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/12/50/d255d4ac46ae860c7efb79114546/pollion-v-cta-filed-cal.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>
entries.author: Kaitlin Washburn
